explanation:
The patient has presented with features of small bowel obstruction,
namely the abdominal pain which is relieved by vomiting. It is important
to remember that abdominal distension may be absent in small bowel
obstruction (SBO). The most common cause of SBO is intra-abdominal
adhesions, accounting for the majority of cases, followed by hernias and
inflammatory structures (e.g. Crohn disease). Rarer causes include
gallstone ileus.
The past medical history of recurrent cholecystitis, evidence of
pneumobilia (air in the biliary tree), and the presence of SBO makes
gallstone ileus the most likely unifying diagnosis. Gallstone ileus is an
uncommon cause of a mechanical small bowel obstruction. It is a rare
complication of chronic cholecystitis and occurs when a gallstone
passes through a fistula between the gallbladder and small bowel before
becoming impacted at the ileocaecal valve.
The amylase is only mildly raised and certainly not high enough to be
diagnostic of pancreatitis. It is important to remember that amylase is
non-specific and can be raised due to a variety of processes. Although
pancreatitis can cause a sentinel loop, which is a short segment of
adynamic ileus close to an intra-abdominal inflammatory process, it
would not cause a small bowel obstruction.
A paraduodenal abscess and emphysematous cholangitis can also
cause pneumobilia, however they would not result in small bowel
obstruction, making gall stone ileus a better answer.
Gallstone ileus is a mechanical small bowel obstruction which
occurs due a gallstone obstruction most often in the ileum

explanation:
Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole is the correct option. The patient
has experienced treatment failure of Clostridium difficile infection as
demonstrated by ongoing diarrhoea and persisting detectable toxin in
the stool. The 3rd line option to treat the infection in this circumstance is
oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole.
Colectomy is incorrect. This option would only be used in the setting of
life-threatening disease. There is no documentation to suggest that is
the case here.
Faecal transplant is incorrect. While this is an option for treating
recurrent Clostridium difficile infection, it is only used after more
conservative measures have been exhausted.
IV vancomycin is incorrect. This method of administering vancomycin is
ineffective in Clostridium difficile infection and should not be used.
If a first episode of C. difficile doesn't respond to either vancomycin
or fidaxomicin then oral vancomycin +/- IV metronidazole should be
tried
Repeat oral fidaxomicin is incorrect. Repeating a course of oral
vancomycin rather than fidaxomicin is a recognized option.
Clostridioides difficile
Clostridioides difficile is a Gram positive rod often encountered in
hospital practice. It produces an exotoxin which causes intestinal
damage leading to a syndrome called pseudomembranous colitis. C.
difficile develops when the normal gut flora are suppressed by broad-
spectrum antibiotics. Clindamycin is historically associated with causing
C. difficile but the aetiology has evolved significantly over the past 10
years. Second and third-generation cephalosporins are now the leading
cause of C. difficile.
Other than antibiotics, risk factors include:
proton pump inhibitors
Pathophysiology
anaerobic gram-positive, spore-forming, toxin-producing bacillus
transmission: via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores
releases two exotoxins (toxin A and toxin B) that act on intestinal
epithelial cells and inflammatory cells resulting in colitis
Features
diarrhoea
abdominal pain
a raised white blood cell count (WCC) is characteristic
if severe toxic megacolon may develop

Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition which can ultimately
affect both the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas.
Around 80% of cases are due to alcohol excess with up to 20% of cases
being unexplained.
Other than alcohol, causes include:

ductal obstruction: tumours, stones, structural abnormalities
including pancreas divisum and annular pancreas

syndromes, particularly bile salt malabsorption, leading to persistent
diarrhoea. The treatment is with oral cholestyramine which is a bile acid
sequestrant. This acts by binding bile salts, making them insoluble,
preventing them from creating an osmotic shift of water into the large
bowel and so helping to prevent diarrhoea.
Oral mesalazine is used in the treatment of Crohn's disease, such as
mild flares. The normal blood test results do not suggest a flare and
therefore this answer is incorrect.
Oral metronidazole is an antibiotic that can be used for some
gastrointestinal infections, such as Clostridioides difficile or giardiasis.
There is no suggestion of these infections from the history, therefore this
answer is incorrect.
Prednisolone may be used in flares of Crohn's disease, however, the
normal blood test results mean this diagnosis is less likely. Therefore,
both oral prednisolone and rectal prednisolone are incorrect.

explanation:
The results above represent a hepatocellular cause of jaundice. This is
shown from the elevated unconjugated bilirubin levels and differentiates
it from a post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice. All of the agents above can
cause a cholestatic (obstructive) picture but the most likely cause of a
hepatocellular jaundice is nitrofurantoin. This occurs with chronic use of
the medication. It is associated with hepatic necrosis and should be
stopped immediately when there is any evidence of hepatic necrosis.
The side effects of nitrofurantoin can be fatal and as such attention
must be paid to its appearance on a drug history. Toxic effects can
manifest as hepatic disease as shown here but also as both an acute
and chronic respiratory condition, agranulocytosis and the acute
hypersensitivity reaction of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
There is no clear guidance in the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in adult
patients. However, recent Cochrane review questioned the use in
children. The other common advice given to patients is to drink
cranberry juice to prevent further infections, but this again has not been
backed up by the study data. Therefore there is currently no consensus,
but recurrent UTI should warrant further investigations by either a
gynaecologist or urologist in adults and most certainly a paediatrician in
children.
Drug-induced liver disease
Drug-induced liver disease is generally divided into hepatocellular,
cholestatic or mixed. There is however considerable overlap, with some
drugs causing a range of changes to the liver
The following drugs tend to cause a hepatocellular picture:
paracetamol
sodium valproate, phenytoin
MAOIs
halothane
anti-tuberculosis: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide
statins
alcohol
amiodarone

This man is suffering from septic shock and end-organ damage
secondary to the hypoperfusion. This is evidenced by the deranged LFTs
and AKI. Therefore ischaemic hepatitis is the most likely diagnosis.
Co-amoxiclav is known to cause cholestatic liver injury. If this was the
cause, the ALP would be proportionally higher compared to the ALT.
There is no question that the patient is septic with the presentation of
fever, tachycardia, hypotension and raised inflammatory markers.
However, there is no evidence of abdominal pain; and the symptoms and
x-ray finding are in keeping with community-acquired pneumonia
therefore biliary sepsis is not the most likely cause.
Alcoholic hepatitis would be associated with a greater increase in
bilirubin. There is also no evidence provided to support alcohol misuse.
Whilst we know that patient had been taking paracetamol, there are no
details indicating overdose. In these situations, it would be good practice
to check paracetamol levels.
Acute hypoperfusion (e.g. low BP secondary to blood loss) may
result in ischaemic hepatitis
Ischaemic hepatitis
Ischaemic hepatitis is a diffuse hepatic injury resulting from acute
hypoperfusion (sometimes known as 'shock liver'). It is not an
inflammatory process. It is diagnosed in the presence of an inciting
event (e.g. a cardiac arrest) and marked increases in aminotransferase
levels (exceeding 1000 international unit/L or 50 times the upper limit of
normal). Often, it will occur in conjunction with acute kidney injury
(tubular necrosis) or other end-organ dysfunction.

explanation:
This patient has bile acid malabsorption following extensive terminal
ileal and small bowel resection for his Crohn's disease. A complication
of extensive terminal ileal resection is bile acid diarrhoea which presents
with watery loose stools including nocturnal episodes. The diagnostic
test is the SeHCAT scan (nuclear medicine) which used radiolabelled
selenium and measures the retention of the labelled molecule. BAD is
diagnosed by a <15% retention of SeHCAT at 7 days.
The treatment is with bile acid sequestrants including cholestyramine
(Questran). This is the correct answer here, the patient does not have an
acute flare so Infliximab frequency does not need altering. Loperamide
and codeine will not treat the underlying cause and octreotide can be
used to treat diarrhoea in VIPomas.
Ongoing diarrhoea in Crohn's patient post-resection with normal
CRP → cholestyramine
Cholestyramine
Cholestyramine is a bile acid sequestrant used in the management of
hyperlipidaemia. It decreases bile acid reabsorption in the small
intestine, therefore upregulating the amount of cholesterol that is
converted to bile acid. The main effect it has on the lipid profile is to
reduce LDL cholesterol. It is also occasionally used in Crohn's disease
for treatment diarrhoea following bowel resection.
Adverse effects
abdominal cramps and constipation
decreases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
cholesterol gallstones
may raise level of triglycerides

Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary
cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged
females (female:male ratio of 9:1). The aetiology is not fully understood
although it is thought to be an autoimmune condition. Interlobular bile
ducts become damaged by a chronic inflammatory process causing
progressive cholestasis which may eventually progress to cirrhosis. The
classic presentation is itching in a middle-aged woman
Associations
Sjogren's syndrome (seen in up to 80% of patients)
rheumatoid arthritis
systemic sclerosis
thyroid disease

early: may be asymptomatic (e.g. raised ALP on routine LFTs) or

options: Urea and electrolytes, including phosphate and magnesium
explanation:
Alcoholic patients are often malnourished. In hospital the patient has
(hopefully!) no access to alcohol but also three meals a day provided.
Re-feeding syndrome is the only condition responsible for the above
symptoms that can be readily diagnosed from the above tests. Blood
tests will reveal electrolyte disturbances particularly hypophsphataemia
accompanying the neurological and pulmonary manifestations.
Treatment involves replacing the depleted electrolytes and slow build up
of diet.

see him because of acute shortness of breath and generalised muscle
weakness. On examination his blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, pulse is
86 beats per minute and regular. He has bilateral crackles on

Question 78 of 267
A 49-year-old man with a history of alcoholism has been admitted to the
ward for a detoxification program. He was brought to the hospital by
police in an intoxicated state. He has been treated with B vitamin
replacement therapy and has now begun re-feeding. You are asked to
see him because of acute shortness of breath and generalised muscle
weakness. On examination his blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, pulse is
86 beats per minute and regular. He has bilateral crackles on
auscultation of his chest consistent with heart failure, and global 4/5
power weakness.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Globalised muscle weakness coupled with symptoms of heart failure is
consistent with re-feeding syndrome. This occurs because of intra-
cellular movement of phosphate, thought to be related to be related to
hyperinsulinaemia because of carbohydrate loading. Heart failure and
muscle weakness can be avoided by ensuring that any feeds used
contain adequate phosphate when used in the treatment of patients at
risk of re-feeding syndrome, such as those with alcoholism and / or
eating disorders.
Low thiamine results in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Although low
potassium can result in muscle weakness and is seen in reactive
hyperinsulinaemia, feeds normally contain adequate potassium to avoid
this, hence it's less likely than hypophosphataemia in this situation.
Folate deficiency is manifest by anaemia, glossitis, and neuropathy, and
magnesium deficiency presents with similar symptoms to
hypocalcaemia.
Refeeding syndrome
Refeeding syndrome describes the metabolic abnormalities which occur
on feeding a person following a period of starvation. It occurs when an
extended period of catabolism ends abruptly with switching to
carbohydrate metabolism. The metabolic consequences include:
hypophosphataemia
this is the hallmark symptom of refeeding syndrome
may result in significant muscle weakness, including
myocardial muscle (→ cardiac failure) and the diaphragm (→
respiratory failure)
hypokalaemia
hypomagnesaemia: may predispose to torsades de pointes
abnormal fluid balance
Pathophysiology of Hypophosphatemia in Refeeding Syndrome:
Shift from Fat to Carbohydrate Metabolism: In refeeding syndrome,
the reintroduction of carbohydrates leads to a shift from fat to
carbohydrate metabolism. This switch activates insulin secretion,
which in turn increases cellular uptake of glucose.

A 58-year-old female was referred to the gastroenterology clinic. Her GP
had detected on routine blood investigations deranged liver function
testing which despite repeated testing was found to be persistent. Her
past medical history comprised diabetes mellitus type 2 diagnosed
twelve years ago. Unfortunately, this was poorly controlled, despite the
use of metformin 500mg TDS, glitazone 160mg OD, pioglitazone 15mg
OD, aspirin 75mg OD and Lantus 42 units OD. She also suffered from

Pentasa.
Today, he reports his symptoms have not improved despite treatment.
He is still opening his bowels 5 times per day and is concern about it.
He is mildly dehydrated clinically, but haemodynamically stable, with a
blood pressure of 120/76 mmHg and a heart rate of 70 beats per
minute. His abdomen is soft and not distended.
What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
This gentleman has symptoms of moderate ulcerative colitis which was
not managed with oral 5 ASA. He is not on topical therapy following an
initial assessment which gives you the clue that his disease is not
isolated to proctitis.
His symptoms are still that of moderate ulcerative colitis and given his
failure to respond to treatment he should now be started on oral
prednisolone with a follow up in 2 weeks for re-review of symptoms.
Mild to moderate ulcerative colitis ( up to 6 motions per day with mild
bleed. ESR <30) should be managed using a stepwise approach.
Proctitis: Induce remission with a topical 5-ASA (aminosalicylic
acid). If no response or cant tolerate, 5-ASA the next step would be
to add topical steroids. Oral should be considered if remission not
achieved or patient presents with left-sided extensive ulcerative
colitis.
Left-sided extensive disease should be managed using oral 5-ASA
initially with or without topical 5-ASA. If no improvement within 4
weeks oral prednisolone therapy should be added. If no response to
oral prednisolone, tacrolimus should be started to induce remission.

Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Acute upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a common and important
presentation. It may be caused by a wide variety of conditions but is
most commonly due to either oesophageal varices or peptic ulcer
disease.

A 55-year-old man attends the emergency department following a
collapse at a family barbecue. Prior to the collapse, he complained of
feeling dizzy with a fluttering feeling in his chest. He has a past medical
history of hypertension for which he takes amlodipine and ramipril.
On examination, he is alert and oriented. Peripheral pulses are intact
bilaterally and his lying and standing blood pressures are 155/89mmHg
and 147/80mmHg, respectively. On auscultation, his chest is clear and
heart sounds are normal. His neurological examination is unremarkable,
although he still complains of feeling dizzy.
An ECG is taken, as shown below:
© Image used on license from Dr Smith, University of Minnesota
What is the next most immediate step in the management of this
patient?
explanation:
This patient's ECG shows peaked T waves and QRS widening in the
majority of the leads in keeping with hyperkalaemia. Additional ECG
findings include P wave flattening, PR interval prolongation, conduction
blocks and bradyarrhythmias. Hyperkalaemia can cause collapse and
dizziness as experienced by this patient. Furthermore, the medication
history of ramipril puts this patient at a higher risk of developing
hyperkalaemia. The treatment of choice is an infusion of calcium
gluconate to stabilise the cardiac membrane.
Amiodarone is used in the treatment of tachyarrhythmias including atrial
fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. Whilst this patient's ECG features
broad QRS complexes, this patient is not tachycardic with a heart rate of
around 66bpm. Furthermore, the significantly peaked T waves are not
suggestive of a tachyarrhythmia. Rather, they indicate hyperkalaemia.
Synchronised electrical cardioversion is used in the management of
tachyarrhythmias with adverse features (e.g. shock, myocardial
ischaemia, heart failure). Not only does this patient's ECG not represent
a tachyarrhythmia, but there are also no adverse features at present and
this patient is haemodynamically stable.
Transcutaneous pacing would be indicated if this patient's ECG
demonstrated a bradyarrhythmia, particularly one with a significant risk
factor for asystole (e.g. Mobitz type II or complete heart block). It does
not play a role in the treatment of hyperkalaemia.
Although there is an ambiguous QRS morphology on this patient's ECG,
there is no clear ST-segment elevation. Instead, there are significantly
peaked T waves that may give a false impression of ST-segment
elevation. With this in mind, it is unlikely that this patient would benefit
from primary percutaneous coronary intervention.

The patient has presented with alcoholic hepatitis, as evidenced by the
history of excessive alcohol consumption, macrocytosis, and AST:ALT
ratio >2:1. Alcoholic hepatitis almost always presents with clinical
jaundice and the presence of a hepatic bruit is particularly suggestive.
An MDS of > 32 is associated with 50% mortality within 2 months and
indicates the need for treatment. All patients should receive vitamin
replenishment and nutritional support. Patients with alcoholic hepatitis
should be encouraged to consume >2000 kcal per day with
supplementation via NG feeding if necessary.
Prednisolone has been shown in meta-analyses to confer a significant
reduction in 28-day mortality in patients with an MDS >32 or hepatic
encephalopathy, however, there was no demonstrable benefit at 90 days
or at one year. Pentoxifylline may reduce mortality in the presence of
hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) but evidence of efficacy in patients without
HRS is lacking.
Combination therapy with prednisolone and pentoxifylline confers no
additional benefit over treatment with prednisolone alone, whilst the use
of N-acetylcysteine as monotherapy in alcoholic hepatitis is not
recommended. In one randomised controlled trial, combination therapy
with prednisolone and N-acetylcysteine was shown to be superior to
prednisolone monotherapy in reducing mortality at 28 days; largely due
to a reduction in the incidence of HRS and superimposed infection.

His observations are as follows: blood pressure 130/66mmHg, heart

An ultrasound of his liver showed a cyst with a 'sand sign'. You requested
a CT abdomen, the report for which is below.
CT abdomen: A cyst measuring 5cm in diameter can be seen in the right
lobe of the liver. At the periphery of this cyst are two smaller cysts each
measuring 1cm in diameter.
Which of the following would be the most useful in confirming the
diagnosis?
explanation:
Serology for Echinococcus granulosuscan be useful in the
investigation of suspected hydatid cysts
This man has developed multiple hepatic cysts. It is worth considering
other causes, but the most likely in this situation is hydatid disease. The
ultrasound showed 'sand sign', debris within the cyst moving freely and
the CT scan suggests sister cysts. Both of these findings are
characteristic of hydatid disease. The Mediterranean basin is an
endemic area, plus he is a farmer. Both of these would be considered
risk factors. Western blot serology for Echinococcus granulosus is the
confirmatory test and is 80-100% sensitive and 88-96% specific. The cyst
may be having a mass effect on the liver, causing obstructive jaundice in
this man, and hence scleral icterus.
Amoebic abscesses usually present as a single mass in the right lobe,
and though there may be multiple cysts, this is less common. In addition
to this, patients with amoebic abscesses typically have a fever and are
more unwell. It is important to differentiate between amoebic abscesses
and hydatid cysts as the management is very different. Hydatid cysts are
treated with albendazole and usually require surgical excision; whereas
amoebic abscesses are typically treated medically with metronidazole
and tinidazole, followed by a luminal amoebicide to eradicate the cystic
stage.
An HIV test might be suggested if you suspect fungal microabscesses,
as these typically occur in immune-compromised individuals. However,
the CT scan does not indicate microabscesses, and he has no other
features to suggest that he may be immunocompromised.
There is little to suggest tuberculosis.
The percutaneous aspiration would in fact be contraindicated. The
hydatid cyst contains allergens that can precipitate a type 1
hypersensitivity reaction, such as anaphylaxis. Plus, there is a risk of
seeding the daughter cysts through the abdomen. During surgical
excision, the cyst walls must not be ruptured.

explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is the most likely diagnosis due to
the patient’s long-standing IBD, which has a strong association with PSC.
The progressive fatigue, pruritus, and jaundice are classic for
cholestasis, which is further supported by the elevated ALP and direct
bilirubin. The presence of p-ANCA positivity strengthens the diagnosis,
as PSC is often associated with autoimmune markers, despite not being
a classic autoimmune disease. Although ANA positivity is noted, it is
non-specific. Early-stage PSC may not show typical ultrasound findings
due to its limited sensitivity (60–70%), so a normal ultrasound does not
exclude the diagnosis. MRCP or ERCP would provide definitive
confirmation.
Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is less likely in this patient due to the
clinical context, serological findings and the predominantly cholestatic
pattern of liver enzyme elevation (ALP > AST/ALT). AIH typically presents
with markedly elevated ALT and AST levels, which are not seen here.
While AIH may present with a positive ANA, it is usually at higher titres
and often accompanied by other markers, such as anti-smooth muscle
antibodies or anti-liver kidney microsomal antibodies, which are absent
in this case.
Alcohol-related liver disease (ALD) is an important differential given the
patient’s history of chronic alcohol use, but it is less likely because
cholestasis is not a dominant feature of ALD. Alcoholic liver disease
typically presents with AST > ALT in a 2:1 ratio, which is not seen here.
Additionally, pruritus and p-ANCA positivity are not characteristic of ALD,
whereas they are commonly found in PSC. While alcohol can contribute
to liver disease, it does not explain the patient’s clinical picture as well as
PSC does.

not report recent medication use, a key factor in diagnosing DILI.
Without a history of medication exposure, DILI becomes unlikely.
Furthermore, DILI often results in more pronounced liver enzyme
elevations and may have a pattern of liver injury related to specific drugs,
which is not present in this patient.
Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) is unlikely in this case because it is not
typically associated with IBD, unlike primary PSC, which has a well-
established connection to IBD. Additionally, PBC is more commonly
associated with the presence of anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA).
While both PBC and PSC can present with cholestatic liver disease, the
patient's IBD and p-ANCA positivity make PBC a much less likely
diagnosis.
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is a biliary disease of unknown aetiology
characterised by inflammation and fibrosis of intra and extra-hepatic bile
ducts.

A 72-year-old man attends gastroenterology clinic for follow-up after a
recent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. The patient had been referred
by his GP for Barrett's oesophagus screening due to long-standing and
severe gastro-oesophageal reflux symptoms, associated with obesity
and current smoker status.The patient reported suffering from severe
heartburn after eating over the previous 10 years. He had been a regular
user of over the counter anti-acid preparations, but had only sought
medical advice in recent weeks after a close friend was diagnosed with
gastric cancer.
The patient's past medical history included obesity, hypertension, type 2
diabetes mellitus and gout. His regular medications were ramipril,
allopurinol, metformin and gliclazide. The patient denied any drug
allergies or intolerances. His father had undergone a partial gastrectomy
for peptic ulcer disease, but there was no family history of Barrett's
oesophagus or oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
The patient was a retired school teacher who lived with his wife. He had
smoked 10 cigarettes per day throughout his adult life and was
abstinent from alcohol.
Following initial clinic assessment, an upper gastro-intestinal endoscopy
was arranged (results given below). The patient had also been initiated
on high-dose proton-pump inhibitor therapy, which had been associated
with significant improvement in reflux symptoms.
Report from upper gastro-intestinal endoscopy: no evidence of hiatus
hernia; 8 cm segment of circumferential salmon-coloured epithelium
extending above gastro-oesophageal junction (quadrant biopsies taken
as per protocol); no mass lesion or ulceration throughout oesophagus,
stomach or first-part duodenum; mild-moderate oesophagitis and mild
gastritis.
Histology from endoscopic biopsies: flat intestinal metaplasia present in
15 of 16 samples; no evidence of dysplasia or carcinoma.
In addition to continued proton-pump inhibitor treatment, what is
appropriate management of this patient's Barrett's oesophagus?
Endoscopic mucosal resection
Surveillance endoscopy every 3 years
Radiofrequency ablation
Surveillance endoscopy every 1 year
Risk factor modification advice only

explanation:
Screening for Barrett's oesophagus is recommended in individuals with
chronic or severe gastro-oesophageal reflux disease symptoms, who
also have three additional risk factors (out of: age > 50 years, male sex,
white race, obesity, smoking), or who have a family history of Barrett's
oesophagus or oesophageal carcinoma.
The patient in this question has Barrett's oesophagus with intestinal
metaplasia but without dysplasia or intra-mucosal carcinoma. The risk
of progression of non-dysplastic Barrett's oesophagus to oesophageal
adenocarcinoma is 0.33 % annually, meaning that endoscopic
surveillance is recommended over therapy. Recommended frequency for
endoscopic surveillance is every 3-5 years.
In the presence of dysplasia, endoscopic therapy is required due to the
much higher risk of progression to adenocarcinoma (10 % per annually
in high-grade dysplasia). A tissue acquisitive technique such as
endoscopic mucosal resection is required for nodular lesions, with
ablative therapy such as radiofrequency ablation reserved for flat
regions of dysplasia or intra-mucosal carcinoma.
Proton-pump inhibitor therapy is recommended in patients with Barrett's
oesophagus due to several cohort studies suggesting that it reduces the
risk of progression to adenocarcinoma.
Pophali P, Halland M. Barrett's oesophagus: diagnosis and management.
BMJ 2016;353:i2373.
Barrett's oesophagus
Barrett's refers to the metaplasia of the lower oesophageal mucosa, with
the usual squamous epithelium being replaced by columnar epithelium.
There is an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, estimated at
50-100 fold. There are no screening programs for Barrett's - it's typically
identified when patients have an endoscopy for evaluation of upper
gastrointestinal symptoms such as dyspepsia.
Barrett's can be subdivided into short (<3cm) and long (>3cm). The
length of the affected segment correlates strongly with the chances of
identifying metaplasia. The overall prevalence of Barrett's oesophagus is
difficult to determine but may be in the region of 1 in 20 and is identified
in up to 12% of those undergoing endoscopy for reflux.
Histological features
the columnar epithelium may resemble that of either the cardiac
region of the stomach or that of the small intestine (e.g. with goblet
cells, brush border)
Risk factors
gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) is the single strongest
risk factor
male gender (7:1 ratio)
smoking
central obesity
Interestingly alcohol does not seem to be an independent risk factor for
Barrett's although it is associated with both GORD and oesophageal
cancer.

explanation:
This patient's investigations indicate that they have T3N1M0 gastric
carcinoma (Stage IIB disease). Standard of care within the UK for stage
II / III disease would be for neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to radical
surgery. The MAGIC trial demonstrated significant improvement in 5 year
survival for three cycles of pre-operative chemotherapy followed by three
cycles of post-operation chemotherapy compared to surgery alone (36 %
vs 23 %; P = 0.009).
Primary surgical resection is only appropriate for stage 1 tumours.
Endomucosal resection can be considered in some early gastric cancers
(T1a).
Extent of surgical resection depends on tumour location with subtotal
gastrectomy feasible for some distal tumours.
Curative treatment is typically not possible in tumours with local
invasion (T4) or distant metastasis (M1).
Thrumurthy S, Chaudry M, Hochhauser D, Mughal M. The diagnosis and
management of gastric cancer. BMJ 2013;347:6367.
Gastric cancer
Gastric cancer accounts for around 2% of all cancer diagnoses in the
developed world, making it much less common than colorectal and
slightly less common than oesophageal cancer. It is a cancer of older
people (half of patients are > 75 years) and has a male predominance
(2:1).

abnormal liver biochemistry and positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) and

hepatitis as the most likely diagnosis. This patient presents with severe
acute autoimmune hepatitis, characterised by jaundice, an elevated
international normalised ratio (INR), and no hepatic encephalopathy.
Prednisolone is the cornerstone of treatment in such scenarios.
Following initial management with steroids, maintenance therapy
typically includes azathioprine, which is commenced once cholestasis
has resolved.
Liver transplantation is not the correct choice. While liver transplantation
must be considered for any individual with severe acute autoimmune
hepatitis, current indications include acute liver failure, decompensated
cirrhosis or a lack of response to conventional medical treatment. As
this case involves a recent diagnosis without prior therapeutic
intervention and lacks evidence of chronic liver disease or malignancy,
this option is inappropriate.

and increased gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT). The rationale for this
approach is that azathioprine can cause idiosyncratic liver injury and
potentially worsen existing cholestasis.

context. It serves as the first-line treatment for primary biliary

other autoimmune disorders, hypergammaglobulinaemia and HLA B8,

according to the types of circulating antibodies present

explanation:

Hydatid cysts
Hydatid cysts are endemic in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern

granulosus. An outer fibrous capsule is formed containing multiple small
daughter cysts. These cysts are allergens which precipitate a type 1
hypersensitivity reaction.

Question 104 of 267
A 44-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology outpatient with
intractable bloating and flatulence. She has a past medical history of
diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. She takes mycophenolate mofetil.
The examination reveals mild abdominal bloating but a soft abdomen.
Her skin is diffusely thickened.
Given the probable diagnosis, what is the best treatment?
explanation:
Rifaximin is correct. The patient presents with chronic bloating and
flatulence. Given her history of systemic sclerosis, the likely cause is
small bowel bacterial overgrowth (SBBO). The diagnosis can be
confirmed with a hydrogen breath test. In this test, hydrogen exhaled in
the breath is measured using a gas chromatograph. Bacteria colonizing
the large bowel in health and small bowel (in disease) produce hydrogen
by fermentation of unabsorbed carbohydrates. Small amounts of
hydrogen are produced normally from unabsorbed carbohydrates
reaching the colon. Large amounts are produced if there is
malabsorption of carbohydrates in the small intestine (allowing larger
Rifaximin is the treatment of choice for small bowel bacterial
overgrowth syndrome
amounts to reach the colon) or if there are excess bacteria in the small
bowel. The hydrogen produced by bacteria is exhaled in the breath and
can then be measured.
Amoxicillin + metronidazole + omeprazole is incorrect. This is a
treatment regimen for H. pylori eradication. This condition typically
presents with dyspepsia rather than bloating and flatulence.
Creon is incorrect. This treatment is used for patients with pancreatic
exocrine insufficiency. Typically, these patients have steatorrhoea
(characterized by pale, difficult-to-flush stools). Stool abnormalities are
not mentioned here.
Hyoscine butylbromide is incorrect. This is an anti-spasmodic, which
sometimes provides pain relief for irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). While
bloating and flatulence may be features of IBS, buscopan (as it is more
commonly known) will mostly help with pain. Additionally, given her
underlying diagnosis of systemic sclerosis, a significant pathology is
more likely.
Metronidazole is incorrect. This treatment may well be effective for
SBBO but rifaximin is preferred as it demonstrated a significantly higher
decontamination rate when compared with metronidazole.
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome (SBBOS) is a disorder
characterised by excessive amounts of bacteria in the small bowel
resulting in gastrointestinal symptoms.
Risk factors for SBBOS
neonates with congenital gastrointestinal abnormalities

explanation:
The most notable laboratory features is the severe acute kidney injury.
This followed shortly after large volume paracentesis (LVP). LVP is a
major risk factor for paracentesis induced circulatory dysfunction,
especially if the patient has not received a plasma expander.
Paracentesis induced circulatory dysfunction (PICD) is thought to occur
secondary to fluid shifting after large volume (>5 litres) paracentesis,
resulting in decreased circulating volume and renal dysfunction.
PICD is definitively diagnosed through laboratory results, with increases
of more than 50% of baseline plasma rennin activity to > 4 ng/mL/h on
the days 5-6 following paracentesis
One of the simplest ways to prevent PICD is to limit the volume of fluid
removed to 5 to 6 L at a time. Current guidelines that recommend that if
> 5 litres of ascitic fluid are removed then albumin should be
administered as a plasma expander.
Paracentesis induced circulatory dysfunction can occur due to large
volume paracentesis (> 5 litres). It is associated with a high rate of
ascites recurrence, development of hepatorenal syndrome,
dilutional hyponatraemia, and high mortality rate
250 cells / mm^3.
Although the patient is in shock, there is nothing to suggest that it is
septic, or haemorrhagic in origin. The patient is in hypovolaemic shock
however it is secondary to PICD which is the best answer in this case.

An 81-year-old man develops abdominal pain in the acute medical unit
having not opened his bowels for four days. It is unclear if he has been
passing flatus however he has not been vomiting. He was admitted
following a fall and is currently receiving analgesia with paracetamol and
codeine as needed and is awaiting nursing home placement. His past
medical history includes Alzheimer's dementia, gout, and
appendicectomy as a child.
On assessment, his respiratory rate is 19/min and oxygen saturations
are 93% on air. His heart rate is 84/min and his blood pressure is
131/90mmHg. Examination of the abdomen reveals a distended,
generally tender abdomen and a rectal examination reveals an empty
rectum. His temperature is 37.1ºC and his Glasgow coma score is 14
due to confusion (which is his baseline).
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
Caecal volvulus
Constipation
Sigmoid volvulus
Small bowel obstruction
Toxic megacolon
Question 106 of 267
An 81-year-old man develops abdominal pain in the acute medical unit
having not opened his bowels for four days. It is unclear if he has been
passing flatus however he has not been vomiting. He was admitted
following a fall and is currently receiving analgesia with paracetamol and
codeine as needed and is awaiting nursing home placement. His past
medical history includes Alzheimer's dementia, gout, and
appendicectomy as a child.
On assessment, his respiratory rate is 19/min and oxygen saturations
are 93% on air. His heart rate is 84/min and his blood pressure is
131/90mmHg. Examination of the abdomen reveals a distended,
generally tender abdomen and a rectal examination reveals an empty
rectum. His temperature is 37.1ºC and his Glasgow coma score is 14
due to confusion (which is his baseline).
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This man has a sigmoid volvulus as confirmed on his abdominal x-ray
which shows the classic coffee bean sign. Note that a sigmoid volvulus
will not retain haustra and typically originate in the left lower quadrant
and extend to the right upper quadrant as is the case here.
A caecal volvulus will typically originate in the right lower quadrant and
extend to the left upper quadrant. Additionally, caecal volvuli retain
haustra. As both of these features are not present here, a sigmoid
volvulus is a more likely diagnosis.
In constipation, large quantities of faeces can be seen throughout the
bowel however the bowel loops, in this case, are air-filled. This, therefore,
rules out a diagnosis of constipation which is incorrect.
This x-ray displays a coffee bean appearance typical of volvuli rather
than small bowel obstruction. In small bowel obstruction, valvulae
conniventes are seen which are absent in the distended bowel loops
here confirming the pathology is large bowel in origin.
Toxic megacolon is a complication of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
and less commonly, infectious colitis. Both of these diagnoses are
unlikely given the lack of any relevant history here. Additionally, the
radiographic features are specific for a volvulus (coffee bean sign) rather
than toxic megacolon which typically shows dilated large bowel possibly
with thumb-printing.

A 42-year-old woman has been referred due to persistent iron deficiency
anaemia despite oral iron supplements. She has a history of
menorrhagia, depression, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
Medications include ferrous fumarate, tranexamic acid, sertraline, and
amitriptyline. She occasionally takes over-the-counter paracetamol,
ibuprofen, and an antacid solution.
Recent investigations have been normal including endoscopy and
imaging. Up-to-date blood tests confirm ongoing iron deficiency
anaemia.
What is the likely cause for her ongoing iron deficiency?
Amitriptyline
Antacid solution
Ibuprofen
Sertraline
Tranexamic acid

A 42-year-old woman has been referred due to persistent iron deficiency
anaemia despite oral iron supplements. She has a history of
menorrhagia, depression, and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease.
Medications include ferrous fumarate, tranexamic acid, sertraline, and
amitriptyline. She occasionally takes over-the-counter paracetamol,
ibuprofen, and an antacid solution.
Recent investigations have been normal including endoscopy and
imaging. Up-to-date blood tests confirm ongoing iron deficiency
anaemia.
What is the likely cause for her ongoing iron deficiency?
explanation:
Antacid solutions, such as peptac, act by coating the stomach with an
alkaline solution containing magnesium and calcium, thus improving
heartburn symptoms. Unfortunately, this can lead to failed absorption of
Oral iron supplement absorption may be impaired by calcium, zinc
or magnesium containing gastric coating suspensions causing
treatment failure. An alternative route of administration should be
considered
oral iron replacement and is, therefore, the correct answer.
Amitriptyline does not affect oral iron absorption.
Ibuprofen can increase the risk of gastrointestinal (GI) ulceration which
may lead to iron deficiency via bleeding, however, recent endoscopy is
normal and so this is unlikely to be the cause.
Sertraline, as with ibuprofen, carries an increased risk of GI ulceration
and therefore may lead to iron deficiency via bleeding, however again,
recent endoscopy is normal and so this is unlikely to be the cause.
Tranexamic acid is used to control heavy bleeding but is not associated
with impaired iron absorption.

A 30-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic with a flare
of ulcerative colitis. She reports that for the month she has been
experiencing diarrhoea, with bowels opening up to 10 times per day. She
denies any fevers. She has been compliant with mesalazine orally and
has continued her rectal mesalazine variably as she finds the enema
preparations very difficult to administer. She is a non-smoker and works
as a school teacher. Her symptoms are causing her significant
difficulties and she has had several accidents at work, which she found
very distressing.
On clinical assessment, she is afebrile, basic observations are within
normal limits and her abdomen is soft with moderate diffuse
tenderness.
Blood tests show:

bowel dilatation.
A flexible sigmoidoscopy is arranged for the following day and shows
moderate inflammation and is terminated due to patient discomfort.
The patient is admitted and commences a course of intravenous
steroids, which markedly improve her symptoms and within 48 hours she
is stepped down to oral steroids and discharged on day three post-
admission.
Given the clinical history, which of the following interventions should be
considered for this patient once she has recovered from her acute flare?
Continue on oral and rectal mesalazine, no changes
Long term prednisolone

explanation:
This patient has suffered 2 exacerbations in the past year and thus her
current treatment with oral and rectal mesalazine is likely insufficient to
maintain remission.
Long term prednisolone has a huge list of side effects and is not
recommended as risks often outweigh benefits.
The patient's abdominal X-ray showed no features of toxic megacolon or
acute severe inflammation and symptoms settled well with steroids,
thus surgical intervention would not be warranted at this stage.
Infliximab could be considered but carries the risk of immune responses
and significant immunosuppression, thus is generally reserved for
patients with a severe flare not responding to steroids, or in cases that
are unresponsive/intolerant to azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine.
Remember TPMT should be checked in all patients ideally prior to
commencement of either azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine to reduce
the risk of toxicity.
If a patient with ulcerative colitis has had a severe relapse or >=2
exacerbations in the past year they should be given either oral
azathioprine or oral mercaptopurine to maintain remission

A 50-year-old woman with a history of polycythaemia rubra vera
develops abdominal pain and gross ascites over the past 2 months. Due
to her busy work as a lawyer she mentions that her diet is mostly
takeaways, however she is a lifelong teetotaler.
On examination: mild jaundice with smooth hepatomegaly.
Hepatojugular reflex is negative. Abdominal wall is grossly oedematous
with an associated tortuous venous pattern. There is prominent lower
limb oedema.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Hepatic cirrhosis
Hepatocellular carcinoma
Primary sclerosing cholangitis
Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis
Question 109 of 267
A 50-year-old woman with a history of polycythaemia rubra vera
develops abdominal pain and gross ascites over the past 2 months. Due
to her busy work as a lawyer she mentions that her diet is mostly
takeaways, however she is a lifelong teetotaler.
On examination: mild jaundice with smooth hepatomegaly.
Hepatojugular reflex is negative. Abdominal wall is grossly oedematous
with an associated tortuous venous pattern. There is prominent lower
limb oedema.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Budd-Chiari syndrome occurs when hepatic venous outflow is
obstructed secondary to thrombosis of the major hepatic veins. The
thrombus can extend into the inferior vena cava, leading to the
abdominal wall signs and leg oedema as noted in the presentation. The
condition is rare, typically occurring in the setting of a coagulopathy due
to haematologic disease, which in this cause is polycythaemia rubra
vera. The impression from the patient's social history may lead you
Budd-Chiari syndrome presents with the triad of sudden onset
abdominal pain, ascites, and tender hepatomegaly
towards considering nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, however this does not
cause ascities.
Budd-Chiari syndrome
Budd-Chiari syndrome, or hepatic vein thrombosis, is usually seen in the
context of underlying haematological disease or another procoagulant
condition.

This patient has a diagnosis of autoimmune pancreatitis. Clinical
features suggestive of pancreatitis from this scenario include jaundice,
nausea and pancreatic enlargement on the abdominal CT scan. Unlike
acute pancreatitis that typically presents with abdominal pain and
vomiting, autoimmune pancreatitis presents differently with symptoms
that include nausea, weight loss and jaundice. In some patients, there
may be extra-pancreatic manifestations or a new diagnosis of diabetes
mellitus. It is associated with autoimmune conditions such as
rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren's syndrome. Antinuclear antibodies and
IgG4 levels are raised in autoimmune pancreatitis and are commonly
used in conjunction with radiographic imaging (such as a CT abdomen
and pelvis) to confirm the diagnosis. Radiographic features of
autoimmune pancreatitis include diffuse enlargement, giving the
appearance of a 'sausage-shaped' pancreas.
Faecal elastase is a useful marker of pancreatic exocrine function. It is
often raised in patients with chronic pancreatitis. Features of chronic
pancreatitis include malaise, weight loss, abdominal pain and
steatorrhoea. It has no role in the diagnosis of autoimmune pancreatitis.
Serum Ca 19-9 levels are used in the diagnosis of pancreatic
malignancy. Patients with painless jaundice (as described in this
question stem) and weight loss should be investigated for pancreatic
malignancy. However, the presence of global pancreatic enlargement
Autoimmune pancreatitis can be diagnosed with a combination of
imaging and raised serum IgG4
over a focal pancreatic mass on this patient's CT imaging combined with
a past medical history of autoimmune disease makes pancreatic cancer
less likely.
Unlike acute pancreatitis, serum amylase is not necessarily elevated in
autoimmune pancreatitis, and therefore it is not the most sensitive
diagnostic marker to request.
Transferrin saturation is used in the diagnosis of haemochromatosis, an
autosomal recessive disorder of iron absorption. Iron can accumulate in
the pancreas to give rise to diabetes mellitus and in the liver to cause
chronic liver disease. Other common symptoms include arthralgia and
bronze skin pigmentation that are not described here.

A 47-year-old lady presents to the Emergency Department with large-
volume haematemesis. The blood is bright red and she reports
experiencing 3 separate episodes over the preceding 12 hours. Despite a
previous diagnosis of alcoholic liver disease, she continues to drink a
bottle of vodka per day.
On examination, she is pale and clammy. Her pulse is 128bpm and her
blood pressure is 87/58mmHg. Her chest is clear and her heart sounds
are normal. Her abdomen is distended with mild right upper quadrant
tenderness and evidence of shifting dullness.
She is resuscitated with intravenous fluids and 4 units of cross-matched
blood are requested. Terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone are
administered whilst an emergency endoscopy is arranged. She
subsequently undergoes variceal band ligation and returns to the ward,
where she passes an uneventful night.
Over the next few days, she has two further episodes of large-volume
haematemesis which are only partly controlled by repeat endoscopic
intervention. She is reviewed by the Gastroenterology Consultant and a
plan to refer the patient for a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic
shunt (TIPSS) is made.
Which of the following is the greatest contraindication to a TIPSS
procedure?
Child-Pugh class A liver disease
Hepatic encephalopathy
INR 1.7
Refractory ascites
Pleural effusion
Question 111 of 267
A 47-year-old lady presents to the Emergency Department with large-
volume haematemesis. The blood is bright red and she reports
experiencing 3 separate episodes over the preceding 12 hours. Despite a
previous diagnosis of alcoholic liver disease, she continues to drink a
bottle of vodka per day.
On examination, she is pale and clammy. Her pulse is 128bpm and her
blood pressure is 87/58mmHg. Her chest is clear and her heart sounds
are normal. Her abdomen is distended with mild right upper quadrant
tenderness and evidence of shifting dullness.
She is resuscitated with intravenous fluids and 4 units of cross-matched
blood are requested. Terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone are
administered whilst an emergency endoscopy is arranged. She
subsequently undergoes variceal band ligation and returns to the ward,
where she passes an uneventful night.
Over the next few days, she has two further episodes of large-volume
haematemesis which are only partly controlled by repeat endoscopic
intervention. She is reviewed by the Gastroenterology Consultant and a
plan to refer the patient for a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic
shunt (TIPSS) is made.
Which of the following is the greatest contraindication to a TIPSS
procedure?
explanation:
A TIPSS procedure involves the percutaneous creation of a low-pressure
tract between the intrahepatic portal vein and the hepatic vein. This
allows blood to bypass the liver and lowers portal pressure. The primary
indications for TIPSS include uncontrolled variceal haemorrhage,
refractory ascites, and hepatic pleural effusion.
Absolute contraindications for TIPSS include:
Severe and progressive liver failure (Child-Pugh score >12 is
associated with a high risk of early death)
Uncontrolled hepatic encephalopathy
Right-sided heart failure
Uncontrolled sepsis
Unrelieved biliary obstruction
Relative contraindications:
Severe uncorrectable coagulopathy (INR >5)
Thrombocytopenia <20 * 10 /l
Portal and hepatic vein thrombosis
Pulmonary hypertension
Central hepatoma
Taking the above into consideration, we can eliminate options 4 and 5 as
they are actually indications for a TIPSS procedure. Child-Pugh class A
liver disease is not a contraindication to TIPSS and it is debatable
whether an INR of 1.7 would need to be corrected prior to the procedure.
This leaves option 2 as the correct answer.

A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department due to
bleeding from hair follicles on his head. He has also noticed that he has
been off his food and losing weight. He is currently homeless after
having been made redundant from his job one year ago. He is alcohol
dependent with 30-units per week of hard liquor. He is not confused.
He has a past medical history of tuberculosis, for which he completed
treatment six months. This treatment finished two months ago. On
examination, he appears unkempt with poor oral hygiene and gingivitis.
He has global muscle weakness rated at 4+/5 on the MRC scale. There
is no sensory impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Pellagra
Scurvy
Beriberi
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
Recurrence of tuberculosis
Question 112 of 267
A 42-year-old man presents to the emergency department due to
bleeding from hair follicles on his head. He has also noticed that he has
been off his food and losing weight. He is currently homeless after
having been made redundant from his job one year ago. He is alcohol
dependent with 30-units per week of hard liquor. He is not confused.
He has a past medical history of tuberculosis, for which he completed
treatment six months. This treatment finished two months ago. On
examination, he appears unkempt with poor oral hygiene and gingivitis.
He has global muscle weakness rated at 4+/5 on the MRC scale. There
is no sensory impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The correct answer is scurvy. He is a homeless and alcohol-dependent
patient who is very likely to have a very poor diet. The combination of
bleeding hair follicles and gingivitis is highly suggestive of vitamin C
(ascorbic acid) deficiency. Pellagra is associated with diarrhoea and
dementia. Beriberi can be associated with peripheral neuropathy with
sensory involvement, or heart failure and oedema. Neither of these
cases is described here. The classical triad of nystagmus,
ophthalmoplegia and ataxia with confusion is not described, making
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome less likely. The absence of a cough,
haemoptysis and night sweats makes TB recurrence less likely.
Vitamin C deficiency (scurvy)
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is found in citrus fruits, tomatoes, potatoes,
Brussel sprouts, cauliflower, broccoli, cabbage and spinach. Deficiency
(commonly called scurvy) leads to impaired collagen synthesis and
disordered connective tissue as ascorbic acid is a cofactor for enzymes
used in the production of proline and lysine. It is associated with severe
malnutrition as well as drug and alcohol abuse, and those living in
poverty with limited access to fruits and vegetables.
Symptoms and signs include:
Follicular hyperkeratosis and perifollicular haemorrhage
Ecchymosis, easy bruising
Poor wound healing
Gingivitis with bleeding and receding gums
Sjogren's syndrome
Arthralgia
Oedema
Impaired wound healing
Generalised symptoms such as weakness, malaise, anorexia and
depression

Autoimmune diseases, in this case pernicious anaemia, are more likely
in the presence of another autoimmune disease (rheumatoid arthritis).
Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune condition that targets the parietal
cells of the gastric lining, the role of which is to produce intrinsic factor.
Intrinsic factor is responsible for the absorption of vitamin B12. In this
case, a lack of B12 has led to a macrocytic anaemia as seen with the
high MCV. To diagnose pernicious anaemia blood can be tested for
parietal cell antibodies and intrinsic factor antibodies. These supersede
the classical test Schilling Test.
The patient in this case demonstrated glossitis and angular chelitis with
brittle nails that are associated with this condition. Her blunted affect is
a sign of mild cognitive impairment that can also be present. The signs
and symptoms of pernicious anaemia are vast and there frequency in
clinical practice can be varied. Often the only presentation is with the
fatigue associated with the anaemia.
It should be noted that another treatment for rheumatoid arthritis,
Methotrexate, can induce another type of macrocytic anaemia. This is
due to it inhibiting DNA replication in the same way as heavy metals
such as lead.

is highly suspicious. This is further reinforced by the fact that this man's
ALT is more markedly deranged than his AST.
Alcoholic liver disease is less likely as his drinking only slightly exceeds
the recommended limit. Additionally, alcoholic liver disease is
associated with a disproportionately deranged AST rather than ALT.

function tests are indicative of a hepatocellular pattern of injury rather
than cholestatic (which would cause a larger rise in ALP and Î³GT). The

incidental finding and the absence of bile duct dilatation further
eliminates biliary colic as a diagnosis.

A 65-year-old woman with a known history of hypertension, ischaemic
heart disease and diabetes was brought in by ambulance after the family
found her collapsed on the bedroom floor. She lives alone and the family
is unsure about the duration the patient was on the floor. Her vital signs
are stable with a pulse rate of 100 bpm and a spot hs troponin was
normal. Other blood tests were pending.
Her 12 lead ECG shows:
© Image used on license from Dr Smith, University of Minnesota
What is the next most important step in her management?
options: Normal saline with added potassium chloride infusion
explanation:
The ECG shows peaked or 'tall-tented' T waves, loss of P waves and
broad QRS complexes with a sinusoidal wave pattern suggestive of
hyperkalaemia.
Calcium gluconate is the correct answer. The ECG changes are
consistent with hyperkalaemia likely secondary to acute renal failure
from a fall, long lie and myoglobinuria. Patients with hyperkalaemia and
ECG changes are at high risk of developing ventricular fibrillation (VF).
Calcium gluconate is a cardiac membrane stabiliser that reduces the
risk of VF and should be promptly administered in this patient.
Magnesium sulphate is the treatment of choice for torsades de pointes
and may be considered in high burden of recurrent premature ventricular
complexes in ventricular bigeminy or trigeminy which are not seen in this
patient.
Normal saline with added potassium chloride infusion is the treatment
of choice in hypokalaemia. Hypokalaemia causes typical ECG changes
of widespread ST depression, T wave inversion, and prominent U waves
which are not seen in this patient.
Percutaneous coronary intervention is the treatment of choice for ST
elevation myocardial infarction. ECG changes in hyperkalaemia can
mimic STEMI as seen in this ECG but the normal hs troponin makes
STEMI less likely.
Transcutaneous pacing is used in patients with symptomatic
bradyarrhythmia while they await a permanent pacemaker insertion. This
patient does not have bradyarrhythmia and has a perfusion pulse rate of
100bpm. Hence pacing is not indicated in this patient.

Barrett's oesophagus
Barrett's refers to the metaplasia of the lower oesophageal mucosa, with
the usual squamous epithelium being replaced by columnar epithelium.
There is an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma, estimated at
50-100 fold. There are no screening programs for Barrett's - it's typically
identified when patients have an endoscopy for evaluation of upper
gastrointestinal symptoms such as dyspepsia.
Barrett's can be subdivided into short (<3cm) and long (>3cm). The
length of the affected segment correlates strongly with the chances of
identifying metaplasia. The overall prevalence of Barrett's oesophagus is
difficult to determine but may be in the region of 1 in 20 and is identified
in up to 12% of those undergoing endoscopy for reflux.

The history of fatigue and itching in an otherwise-well middle-aged
female patient, with a background of autoimmune disease, strongly
points towards primary biliary cholangitis. This is supported by the
elevated LFTs, in particular the ALP and gamma-GT. Subsequent testing
would involve screening for anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA), which
are highly specific, present in 98% of patients. First-line treatment
involves the use of ursodeoxycholic acid, which slows disease
progression and improves symptoms.
Cetirizine is an antihistamine. Whilst generally used to relieve symptoms
of itching in numerous conditions, given that the underlying diagnosis
here is primary biliary cholangitis, ursodeoxycholic acid is the more
definitive management, and cetirizine may be used as an adjunct for
symptom relief.
Cholestyramine may be used as an adjunct to help with the relief of
pruritus. However, it does not play a role in the management of disease
progression - ursodeoxycholic acid is used for this initially.
Fexofenadine is another antihistamine, similar to cetirizine. Unlike
cetirizine, it is not available over-the-counter and requires a prescription.
Again, it would not routinely be used in the management of primary
biliary cholangitis.

The management of hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is notoriously difficult.
The ideal treatment is liver transplantation but patients are often too
unwell to have surgery and there is a shortage of donors
The most accepted theory regarding the pathophysiology of HRS is that
vasoactive mediators cause splanchnic vasodilation which in turn
reduces the systemic vascular resistance. This results in 'underfilling' of
the kidneys. This is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus which then
activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, causing renal
vasoconstriction which is not enough to counterbalance the effects of
the splanchnic vasodilation.

He is referred for an oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy and colonoscopy

normal mucosa.

explanation:
The normal endoscopic and histological findings help to narrow our list
of differentials in this patient. A diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome
(IBS) could be considered, but, he has several risk factors for small
bowel bacterial overgrowth. Risk factors are:
Rifaximin is the treatment of choice for small bowel bacterial
overgrowth syndrome
Motility delay, such as diabetes, scleroderma
Anatomical, such as strictures
Immune-related, such as IgA deficiency
Rifaximin is correct as this is the treatment of choice for small bowel
bacterial overgrowth syndrome. A trial of treatment can be used as a
diagnostic tool. The alternative is using the hydrogen breath test.
Avoiding gluten would be correct if celiac disease was the diagnosis,
however, the lack of characteristic histological findings makes this
unlikely.
Creon is a pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy used in pancreatic
insufficiency. This would be more likely if there were steatorrhoea or
weight loss due to malabsorption.
Mesalazine is used in the management of inflammatory bowel disease
(IBD). The normal endoscopic and histological findings make IBD
unlikely.
Omeprazole can be used in gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD)
which typically presents with heartburn and regurgitation symptoms.
These are not present in this case and hence omeprazole is not of
benefit.
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome (SBBOS) is a disorder
characterised by excessive amounts of bacteria in the small bowel
resulting in gastrointestinal symptoms.

She is started on intravenous hydrocortisone. After 72 hours of
treatment, she continues to have 7-8 bloody stools per day, persistent
fever, and tachycardia. Her CRP has risen to 95 mg/L.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
If a severe flare of UC has not responded to IV steroids after 72
hours, consider adding IV ciclosporin or surgery
This patient has a severe flare of ulcerative colitis that has failed to
respond to 72 hours of intravenous steroid therapy, as evidenced by her
ongoing symptoms (7-8 bloody stools per day), persistent fever and
tachycardia, and rising inflammatory markers. In this scenario, the most
appropriate next step is to add intravenous ciclosporin. According to UK
guidelines (NICE and BSG), patients with severe ulcerative colitis who
fail to respond to intravenous steroids after 72 hours should be
considered for either intravenous ciclosporin or surgery. Ciclosporin acts
as a calcineurin inhibitor and has a rapid onset of action, making it
suitable for acute severe colitis. Studies have shown that approximately
60-85% of patients with steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis will respond
to intravenous ciclosporin, potentially avoiding the need for immediate
colectomy. The usual approach is to start with 2 mg/kg/day as a
continuous infusion with close monitoring of ciclosporin levels and renal
function. If the patient responds, they can be transitioned to oral
ciclosporin and then to a longer-term immunosuppressant such as
azathioprine or mercaptopurine.
Add oral azathioprine is not the correct answer in this acute setting.
While azathioprine is an appropriate maintenance therapy for preventing
relapses in ulcerative colitis, particularly after severe flares, it has a slow
onset of action (typically 2-3 months) and is not effective for inducing
remission in acute severe colitis. It would be inappropriate to rely on
azathioprine in this patient who is showing signs of ongoing severe
disease despite intravenous steroids.
Change to oral prednisolone would be a step down in therapy and is
inappropriate for this patient who is failing to respond to more potent
intravenous steroids. Switching to oral steroids would likely result in
further clinical deterioration and increased risk of complications such as
toxic megacolon or perforation. This option would be considered a
management error in a patient with ongoing severe disease.
Commence infliximab is a reasonable alternative to ciclosporin in some
cases of steroid-refractory ulcerative colitis. However, in the UK, NICE
guidelines traditionally recommend ciclosporin as the first-line rescue
therapy, with infliximab typically reserved for patients who have
contraindications to ciclosporin or in centers with more experience using
infliximab in this setting. While practice patterns are evolving, and some
centers may prefer infliximab, ciclosporin remains the standard first-line
rescue therapy according to UK guidelines.
Refer for colectomy is an important option to consider in severe
ulcerative colitis unresponsive to medical therapy, and indeed may be
necessary if the patient fails to respond to ciclosporin. However, it is
generally appropriate to try medical rescue therapy with ciclosporin
before proceeding to surgery, unless there are signs of impending or
actual perforation, toxic megacolon, or massive hemorrhage. This
patient, while not responding to steroids, does not show signs of these
immediate surgical indications, so a trial of ciclosporin would be
appropriate before proceeding to colectomy.

narrowed distal oesophageal lumen caused by webs that are ruptured as

options: Treatment includes iron supplementation and dilation of the webs Pharyngeal carcinoma
explanation:
Oesophageal webs in association with iron deficiency anaemia (resulting
in clinical glossitis and koilonychia) and dysphagia is Plummer-Vinson
syndrome, particularly prevalent in middle-aged white Caucasian
females. The post cricoid oesophageal webs are premalignant for
oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and pharyngeal SCC,
which instead of webs on OGD, present as plaques, nodules or ulcerated
masses instead. However, the agreed frequency of follow-up OGD
monitoring is debated in Plummer-Vinson syndrome. Frequently, the
webs recede on iron replacement and break on the scope passing
through, improving dysphagia. Infrequently, dilation may be required, as
in oesophageal rings, caused by mucosal out folds most frequently as a
result of chronic oesophageal reflux and hence, treated in conjunction
with proton pump inhibitors.

A 55-years-old male presents with a 4 week history of persistent
diarrhoea and transient shortness of breath, which he describes to have
been very similar to his childhood asthma. He has no other past medical
history, is a builder and smokes 10 cigarettes per day for the past 30
years. He drinks minimal alcohol. On examination, you note the patient
has a very red face, no clubbing and soft and non-tender abdomen.
Cardiovascular examination reveals a mid diastolic murmur loudest at
the left sternal border. Respiratory examination is unremarkable. blood
pressure is 86/49 mmHg, heart rate 112 beats/min, sats 96% on air and
respiratory rate 20 breaths/ min. Which test is most likely to be
diagnostic?
explanation:
The patient presents with the diarrhoea, tricuspid stenosis, facial
flushing, bronchospasm and hypotension, clearly pointing towards a
unifying diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. However, screening for
carcinoid syndrome should be performed with 24 hour urinary 5HIAA,
the end product of serotonin metabolism. Although well-differentiated
carcinoid tumours secrete elevated levels of plasma chromogranin A, it
is increasingly recognised that falsely positive elevated levels can be
produced by other neuroendocrine tumours, hyperthyroidism,
hyperparathyroidism, pituitary tumours, colon carcinoma, IBD,
hypertension, COPD, ACS amongst many others. The low specificity of
the test means that it is recommended that it is not used on its own as a
screening test.
Urinary serotonin may also be useful but is criticised for low sensitivity
for foregut carcinoid tumours, which often lack aromatic amino acid
decarboxylase to produce 5HIAA. Although current guidelines
recommend the measurement of both 24hr urinary 5HIAA and plasma
chromogranin A , 24 urinary 5HIAA is therefore most likely to be
diagnostic.
1. Ramage JK, Davies AH, ARdill et al. Guidelines for the management of
gastroenterpancreatic neuroendocrine (including carcinoid) tumours.
Gut 2005; 54: 1-16

Carcinoid syndrome
usually occurs when metastases are present in the liver and release
serotonin into the systemic circulation
may also occur with lung carcinoid as mediators are not 'cleared' by
the liver
Features

diarrhoea
bronchospasm
hypotension
right heart valvular stenosis (left heart can be affected in bronchial

other molecules such as ACTH and GHRH may also be secreted
resulting in, for example, Cushing's syndrome

serotonin by the tumour

This lady has a history strongly suggestive of coeliac disease which GP
the erroneously diagnosed as IBS; a common mistake to make. Of note
her anti-endomysial antibody screening test was negative. This test has

is therefore to proceed to OGD and biopsy; whilst a gluten exclusion diet

where possible.

A 56-year-old man has had a recent colonoscopy for per rectal bleeding
which found 2 small adenomas <10mm in size. He has been otherwise
well and does not have a family history of colorectal cancer. What is the
best option for colonoscopic surveillance in this patient?
explanation:
The guidance for colonoscopic surveillance is dependent on the patient's
risk profile and can be divided into low risk, intermediate risk, and high
risk. A patient with 2 small adenomas <10mm in size is at a low risk of
developing colorectal cancer. Therefore a repeat colonoscopy should be
offered at 5 years.
Patients at intermediate risk should be offered a colonoscopy at 3 years
and patients at high risk should be offered a colonoscopy at 1 year.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome
Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disorder
resulting in hyperbilirubinaemia (conjugated, therefore present in urine).
It is due to a defect in the canillicular multispecific organic anion
transporter (cMOAT) protein. This causes defective hepatic bilirubin
excretion
Dubin-Johnson Syndrome is characterised by a raised conjugated

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
The patient presents mainly with symptomatic dysphagia with barium
swallow appearance suggestive of diffuse oesophageal spasm (DES).
He appears intolerant of long-acting nitrates. The management of DES is
controversial beyond this point but it is generally accepted that calcium
channel blockers are optimal for those presenting primarily with chest
pain, dysphagia resistant to pharmacological therapies require more
invasive or surgical treatments. Endoscopic Botox is beneficial but may
require multi-level injections and repeat treatments. Widespread
pneumatic dilation, though appearing drastic, is the most appropriate
management for this patient, who reports significant weight loss due to
severe dysphagic symptoms.

dysphagia. He reports a four-week history of relatively sudden-onset
dysphagia to both liquids and solids and describes regurgitation and
intermittent retrosternal pressure. The patient denies weight loss.
The patient examines normally and passes a bedside swallow
assessment.
What is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
Barium swallow
CT chest/abdomen
Chest X-ray
Oesophageal manometry
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD)
Question 139 of 267
A 45-year-old man presents to the acute medical assessment unit with
dysphagia. He reports a four-week history of relatively sudden-onset
dysphagia to both liquids and solids and describes regurgitation and
intermittent retrosternal pressure. The patient denies weight loss.
The patient examines normally and passes a bedside swallow
assessment.
What is the best investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Dysphagia that is initially to both solids and liquids, regurgitation, no
weight loss, and the relatively sudden-onset nature points towards
achalasia.
Oesophageal manometry is the correct answer. It is the gold standard
investigation to diagnose achalasia because it has the highest
sensitivity. Manometry will show a high resting lower oesophageal
pressure.
Barium swallow is the incorrect answer. A barium swallow can be used
Dysphagia, regurgitation, no weight loss → ?achalasia
to diagnose achalasia, but it is not the gold-standard investigation - it
has a lower sensitivity than oesophageal manometry. A barium swallow
would show a dilated oesophagus that tapers smoothly to a beak-like
narrowing at the gastro-oesophageal junction.
CT chest/abdomen is the incorrect answer. A CT cannot be used to
diagnose achalasia because it is a functional not a structural problem.
CT might be considered if there is a suspicion of extra-luminal cancer
that is compressing the oesophagus.
Chest x-ray is the incorrect answer. A chest X-ray would not confirm or
exclude achalasia in the same way as a CT. However, this patient would
likely receive one in their medical assessment to assess for thorax
masses.
Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) is the incorrect answer. An OGD
would be useful to examine for intra-luminal masses or pathologies such
as oesophageal cancer or Barrett's oesophagus but would not show
achalasia as it cannot measure pressure.

Hepatocellular carcinoma is a known complication of chronic liver

Budd-Chiari syndrome can cause decompensation of chronic liver
disease
Decompensated liver disease
There are multiple causes of decompensation in the patient with liver
disease:
Infection - pneumonia, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, viruses
(hepatitis B, C)
Drugs - paracetamol, anaesthetic agents
Toxin - alcohol, Amanita phalloides mushroom
Vascular - Budd-Chiari syndrome, vena-occlusive disease

Constipation

A 17-year-old male presents with a 3-month history of PR bleeding, lower
abdominal pain and left jaw pain. He reports an inability to gain weight
and appears 'skinnier than his friends'. He has no other medical history.
He knows his father and uncle have 'some problems with their bowels
but they don't talk about it'. On examination, he has a body mass index of
14.7 kg/m² and abdomen is soft. PR is negative. Cardiovascular and
respiratory examinations are normal. Limb neurological examination is
unremarkable. However, when testing muscles of mastication, you note
a raised bony mass in his left jaw that is tender in a non-cranial nerve
distribution to palpation. Colonoscopy reveals hundreds of polyps in his
small bowel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This is a difficult question requiring knowledge of a combination of
colorectal polyps with extracolonic manifestations. The presence of
classical osteomas with a familial polyposis syndrome, sometimes also
with cutaneous, adrenal or nasal lesions, is diagnostic of Gardners
syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis. Peutz-Jeghers is
a reasonable differential but its polyps are more frequently associated
with pigmented lesions instead of bony outgrowths. HNPCC increases
the risk of colonic cancer without polyps, a diagnosis of carcinoma,
despite at high risk, cannot be made at this stage without positive
malignant histology.

Ulcerative colitis
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a form of inflammatory bowel disease.
Inflammation always starts at rectum (hence it is the most common site
for UC), never spreads beyond ileocaecal valve and is continuous. The
peak incidence of ulcerative colitis is in people aged 15-25 years and in
those aged 55-65 years.
The initial presentation is usually following insidious and intermittent
symptoms. Features include:
bloody diarrhoea
