worst in the centre of her abdomen, for the last 2 days. She started
vomiting six hours ago and has been unable to keep fluids down. She
has not opened her bowels for 3 days and her abdomen has become
distended. She does not recall passing flatus today.
She is known to have ovarian cancer with metastases to her bones, liver
and peritoneum. She has had a previous abdominal hysterectomy and
bilateral salpingoophorectomy and two previous courses of
chemotherapy. She has no other past medical history.
On examination she has a diffusely tender tympanic abdomen with no
rebound or guarding. She has palpable peritoneal nodules, a 2 cm liver
edge and mild shifting dullness. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. She has
reduced air entry at both lung bases and mild ankle oedema.
An abdominal x-ray demonstrates dilated loops of small bowel and
evidence if ascites. A CT scan of the abdomen with contrast shows
small bowel obstruction with an ileal transition point adjacent to a site of
peritoneal metastasis. Her liver lesions appear stable and there is no
evidence of ureteric obstruction.
An NG tube is inserted and she is started on intravenous fluids and
analgesia.
Which is the best initial measure to help resolve the obstruction?
explanation:
This lady has complete small bowel obstruction related to her
metastatic cancer. Steroids may help to reduce the inflammation
surrounding the tumour and resolve the obstruction.
Bowel rest is an essential component of the treatment of small bowel
obstruction but unlike in cases of obstruction due adhesions, it is
unlikely to resolve the obstruction when used in isolation.
Metoclopramide is a prokinetic anti-emetic used in pseudo-obstruction
to help stimulate the bowel. It should not be used in small bowel
obstruction due to the risk of perforation and an alternative anti-emetic
should be used.
Chemotherapy and surgery are both important considerations to treat
tumour-related bowel obstruction that is not resolving with steroids. This
should be carefully planned with the input of consultant oncologists and
surgeons, with the patient's fitness for these procedures assessed.
Reference: Tuca et al. Malignant bowel obstruction in advanced cancer
patients: epidemiology, management, and factors influencing
spontaneous resolution. Cancer Management and Research. 2012.
Imaging in bowel obstruction
Looking for small and large bowel obstruction is one of the key
indications for performing an abdominal film.

The patient manages her own cleaning business and drinks 20-25 units

At endoscopy a generalised mild gastritis was found. In addition,

kidneys unremarkable.
PET: no evidence of distant metastasis or nodal involvement
Staging laparoscopy: no evidence of peritoneal or metastatic disease
What is the appropriate treatment for this patient's gastric carcinoma?
explanation:
Endomucosal resection can be used to treat gastric cancer confined to
the mucosa (T1a) provided it is less than 2 cm in diameter, of low or
moderate differentiation and with no ulceration or lymphovascular
involement.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is the treatment of choice for stage II and
stage III gastric carcinoma prior to radical surgery. Extent of surgical
resection depends on tumour location with subtotal gastrectomy
feasible for some distal tumours. Radiotherapy is not used as a first-line
treatment of gastric carcinoma.
Thrumurthy S, Chaudry M, Hochhauser D, Mughal M. The diagnosis and
management of gastric cancer. BMJ 2013;347:6367.
Gastric cancer
Gastric cancer accounts for around 2% of all cancer diagnoses in the
developed world, making it much less common than colorectal and
slightly less common than oesophageal cancer. It is a cancer of older
people (half of patients are > 75 years) and has a male predominance
(2:1).
Gastric adenocarcinoma, the most prevalent type of gastric cancer,
arises from the glandular epithelium of the stomach lining.

Question 220 of 267
A 53-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right
upper quadrant pain and fever. He has a past medical history of type 2
diabetes and takes regular metformin.
Observations:
Heart rate 101 beats per minute
Blood pressure 101/54 mmHg
Respiratory rate 20/minute
Oxygen saturations 95% on room air
Temperature 38.4C
On examination, there is tenderness without guarding in the right upper
quadrant.
A CT abdomen with contrast is arranged, which demonstrates a central
low attenuation lesion surrounded by a high attenuation inner rim and a
low attenuation outer ring.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the correct management?
explanation:
Percutaneous drainage + amoxicillin + ciprofloxacin + metronidazole is
the correct answer. The patient presents with fever and right upper
quadrant pain and undergoes a CT scan, which demonstrates the 'double
target sign', which consists of a central low attenuation lesion
surrounded by a high attenuation inner rim and a low attenuation outer
ring. This sign suggests a hepatic abscess. The management of a liver
abscess is with a combination of drainage and antibiotics. Type 2
diabetes is a risk factor for liver abscess development. Most infections
are polymicrobial, consisting of aerobic and anaerobic gram-negative
and positive organisms and therefore the antibiotic choice should be
broad enough to cover these types of organisms.
Percutaneous drainage is incorrect. Drainage alone is not optimal
management, the patient should also be administered antibiotics.
Percutaneous drainage + amoxicillin + ciprofloxacin is incorrect. The
antibiotic choice, in this case, would provide reasonable cover for gram-
positive and negative aerobic organisms but does not provide adequate
coverage against anaerobes.
Percutaneous drainage + benzylpenicillin + metronidazole is incorrect.
This antibiotic choice would provide coverage against gram-positive
organisms and anaerobes. However, it would not be sufficient to cover
all gram-negative organisms.
Percutaneous drainage + flucloxacillin + ciprofloxacin is incorrect.
Flucloxacillin is typically used for skin and soft tissue infections. The
absence of metronidazole means anaerobic coverage is insufficient.
Liver abscesses are generally managed with a combination of
antibiotics & drainage

A 54-year-old male nurse suffers a needlestick injury whilst taking blood
from a patient. The patient has a history of intravenous drug use
however there is no known history of an infectious disease. The nurse
himself has no past medical history. He has recently migrated from India
and is unsure if he has been vaccinated for hepatitis B.
Results from his hepatitis B tests are as follows:

What is his hepatitis B status?
explanation:
This question examines the ability to interpret hepatitis screening
serology.
HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) detects whether a person is
HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, IgG anti-HBc positive - previous
infection, not a carrier
currently infected with hepatitis B.
Anti-HBs (hepatitis B surface antibody) status indicates immunity to the
virus and is therefore present in people with either previous
immunisation or infection.
Anti-HBc (hepatitis B core antibody) indicates previous and/or ongoing
infection with hepatitis B. It can be further subdivided into IgG and IgM
which indicates a timeframe for infection. IgM is present in infection of
<6 months, and IgG in infections of >6 months.
This patient has positive anti-HBs and anti-HBc. This indicates
antibodies to both the surface and core antigens which can only occur
from a previous infection, rather than immunisation. As the surface
antigen is negative, this means he is not a carrier.
An acute infection will have positive surface antigen testing and will be
hepatitis B core antibody positive. As immunity has not been obtained in
acute infection, anti-HBs will be negative.
As with acute infection, those with chronic infection will continue to have
positive HBsAg and anti-HBc but will be negative for anti-HBs as they
have not gained immunity.
Vaccination provides immunity and therefore anti-HBs will be positive.
HBsAg will be negative as the person has not come into contact with the
virus itself, as will anti-HBc.
People with a previous infection will be positive for anti-HBs and anti-
HBc but if they are a carrier, they will also be positive for HBsAg.

Hepatitis B serology
Interpreting hepatitis B serology is a dying art form which still occurs at
regular intervals in medical exams. It is important to remember a few key
facts:
surface antigen (HBsAg) is the first marker to appear and causes
the production of anti-HBs
HBsAg normally implies acute disease (present for 1-6 months)
if HBsAg is present for > 6 months then this implies chronic disease
(i.e. Infective)
Anti-HBs implies immunity (either exposure or immunisation). It is
negative in chronic disease
Anti-HBc implies previous (or current) infection. IgM anti-HBc
appears during acute or recent hepatitis B infection and is present
for about 6 months. IgG anti-HBc persists
HbeAg results from breakdown of core antigen from infected liver
cells as is, therefore, a marker of infectivity. Marker of HBV
replication and infectivity
Example results
previous immunisation: anti-HBs positive, all others negative
previous hepatitis B (> 6 months ago), not a carrier: anti-HBc
positive, HBsAg negative
previous hepatitis B, now a carrier: anti-HBc positive, HBsAg positive

Question 222 of 267
A 48-year-old man has attended the gastroenterology clinic for the
results of recent investigations. He was initially referred by his GP due to
unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, and the regurgitation of food. His
only regular medication includes omeprazole 40mg twice daily.
Blood results were unremarkable.
Oesophagoduodenoscopy (OGD) was performed and biopsies were sent
for histology.
OGD
Endoscope passed successfully to D3 with retroflection in the stomach. The distal
third of the oesophagus displayed 2x circumferential rings with evidence of furrowing.
Small stricture present but no evidence of malignancy. 4x biopsies taken. The stomach
and duodenum appeared normal.
Histopathology
Four specimens were examined. Microscopically, all specimens display
increased eosinophil activity.
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate initial
management?
explanation:
Dietary modification and topical steroids are used in the
management of eosinophilic oesophagitis
The above symptoms of weight loss, dysphagia and food regurgitation
are non-specific and are present in many oesophageal disorders. OGD
findings, however, show circumferential oesophageal rings with
furrowing. These findings in combination with increased eosinophil
activity on histology should point towards the diagnosis of eosinophilic
oesophagitis.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis is a diagnosis made through good symptom
history and the ruling out of other differential diagnoses such as reflux.
Macroscopically, the oesophagus may appear normal, however, OGD
may show reduced vasculature, thick mucosa, mucosal furrows,
strictures and laryngeal oedema. Diagnosis is confirmed through
histology showing increased eosinophil activity and deposition.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis is treated with dietary modifications, in an
attempt to eliminate the causative allergen, and topical corticosteroids,
such as budesonide.
Electrocautery via endoscopy is an older endoscopic practice that was
used for minor endoscopic surgeries, such as polypectomies. It is not
used in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis.
Oesophageal dilatation is a treatment used in patients with eosinophilic
oesophagitis when there are symptoms of dysphagia and endoscopy
shows oesophageal strictures. In the above patient, endoscopy showed
circumferential rings but no evidence of stricturing and so oesophageal
dilatation is not currently required.
Oesophageal stenting is not generally used in the management of
eosinophilic oesophagitis as strictures can form in other areas of the
oesophagus. Oesophageal stenting is more commonly used in
oesophageal malignancy to aid in the symptoms of dysphagia.
The use of systemic corticosteroids, such as prednisolone, has been
shown to be as effective in the management of eosinophilic
oesophagitis when compared to topical steroids. However, systemic
corticosteroids carry an increased side effect profile related to the
systemic effect of the steroids and therefore are not often used. Topical
steroids have a local effect in the oesophagus with only minor systemic
effects.
Eosinophilic oesophagitis
Eosinophilic oesophagitis is characterised by an allergic inflammation of
the oesophagus. An oesophageal biopsy will show dense infiltrate of
eosinophils in the epithelium. Although this disease is relatively poorly
understood, it is thought to be caused by an allergic reaction to ingested
food. The resulting oesophageal inflammation results in pain and
dysphagia, amongst other symptoms.

explanation:
The patient described is most likely suffering from Whipple's disease.
Diagnosis is made with small intestinal biopsy showing macrophages
containing Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) granules infiltrating into the lamina
propria.
Choice 1: Reactive arthritis classically occurs following an infection,
Diarrhoea, weight, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, ophthalmoplegia ?
Whipple's disease
which this patient does not mention.
Choice 2: Sarcoidosis biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas, which is
not mentioned.
Choice 3: On histopathology, ulcerative colitis shows acute and chronic
inflammation of the mucosa leading to crypt abscess formation. Crohn's
disease shows full-thickness inflammation with granuloma and
lymphoid aggregate formation and skip regions. Neither are mentioned
in the biopsy results.
Choice 5: A likely choice, however Coeliac disease biopsy results would
mention lymphocyte infiltration (not macrophage infiltration), villous
atrophy and crypt hyperplasia.
Whipple's disease
Whipple's disease is a rare multi-system disorder caused by Tropheryma
whippelii infection. It is more common in those who are HLA-B27
positive and in middle-aged men.

Question 225 of 267
A 25-year-old man who is normally fit and well presents with a 2-week
history of crampy abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. A colonoscopy
shows erythema and oedema in the distal colon and evidence of
proctitis. He is started on mesalazine. What blood test(s) must be done
prior to its commencement?
options: Renal function and full blood count
Liver function test and full blood count
explanation:
Renal function should be monitored before starting an oral
aminosalicylate, at 3 months and then annually thereafter. This should
be done more often in the presence of renal impairment. Blood disorders
can also occur with mesalazine, and patients should be asked to look
out for bruising, bleeding, purpura, fever and sore throat.
TPMT levels should only be needed on commencement of
mercaptopurine or azathioprine.
Amylase, hepatitis screen and liver function tests are not required in
aminosalicylate therapy monitoring.

explanation:
This patient has acute pancreatitis. While there are multiple causes of
acute pancreatitis, the most common causes include gallstones and
alcohol intake. Less common causes include recent endoscopic
retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), infections such as
mumps and Coxsackie virus, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypocalcaemia,
medications and sphincter of Oddi dysfunction.
It would be very unusual for her alcohol intake or current triglyceride
levels to trigger pancreatitis.
In a significant proportion of cases of pancreatitis, no specific cause is
found (idiopathic).

Question 231 of 267
A 52-year-old man on allopurinol for gout takes 20 mg of prednisolone
per day for Crohn's disease, which was diagnosed 12 months ago. He
has no other comorbidities of note. At present, he has a normal bowel
habit with no loose stools or abdominal pain. He has been on the 20 mg
dose of steroid for 12 months and is gaining significant amounts of
weight. Each time you have reduced his dose to 15 mg, he has
developed diarrhoea up to four times per day and required hospital
admission for intravenous steroid therapy. This has happened three
times in total. You wish to add in a steroid-sparing agent to enable the
taper. Which agent should be avoided owing to significant interaction
with allopurinol?
explanation:
Allopurinol enhances the effects and increases the toxicity of
azathioprine. According to the British National Formulary (BNF), one
should reduce the dose of azathioprine to one-quarter of usual dose, but
in practice, I would recommend talking to your consultant before
combining these two medications. The interaction is significant.
Sometimes, specialists do actually combine the two purposefully in
order to be able to use a lower dose of azathioprine...but this is again a
very specialist area. If you see these two drugs together, alarm bells
should ring and further enquiries should be made.
Incidentally, remember to always check serum thiopurine
methyltransferase (TPMT) levels prior to commencing azathioprine.
Azathioprine is a prodrug of mercaptopurine, a substance that is
subsequently metabolised by several alternative pathways, one of which
involves the enzyme TPMT. Because of our natural genetic variability,
some healthy people will just naturally have a deficiency of TPMT
(around three in a thousand). Such people are at a significant risk of
developing severe, potentially life-threatening, bone marrow toxicity
when treated with conventional doses of azathioprine.

established damage. Removal of one unit per week or two is normally

severe abdominal pain. He is an inpatient being managed for
community-acquired pneumonia and has been in persistent atrial
fibrillation during this admission; however, he is not normally on
anticoagulants. His bowels have been opening regularly and are of a
normal character and he has not vomited. He has a past medical history
of type 2 diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
His oxygen saturations are 95% on 2L oxygen, respiratory rate is 20/min,
heart rate is irregular at 103/min, blood pressure is 98/62mmHg, the
temperature is 37.4ºC, and he remains alert. An abdominal examination
reveals a widespread, exquisitely tender abdomen with some guarding
and rebound tenderness.

normal character and he has not vomited. He has a past medical history
of type 2 diabetes and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
His oxygen saturations are 95% on 2L oxygen, respiratory rate is 20/min,
heart rate is irregular at 103/min, blood pressure is 98/62mmHg, the
temperature is 37.4ºC, and he remains alert. An abdominal examination
reveals a widespread, exquisitely tender abdomen with some guarding
and rebound tenderness.
Which of the following is the best next step in the management of this
patient?
explanation:
Acute mesenteric ischaemia usually requires an immediate
laparotomy, particularly if signs of advanced ischemia e.g.
peritonitis or sepsis
This man is peritonitic as evidenced by the findings of guarding and
rebound tenderness on examination. A diagnosis of acute mesenteric
ischaemia must be considered in cases of sudden onset peritonitis on a
background of atrial fibrillation (particularly when not on
anticoagulation). As this man is particularly unwell, a referral to the
surgical team and immediate laparotomy is indicated and is the correct
answer.
As this man is in persistent atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation is likely to
be indicated in the long term however this has no role in the acute
management of acute mesenteric ischaemia. In fact, as this man is likely
to require an urgent laparotomy, anticoagulation would only act to
increase his risk of intraoperative bleeding.
Emergency gastroscopy would be of use in acute gastrointestinal
bleeding. However, with pain being the primary complaint and bowels
being normal in character, there is no evidence here that this is required.
Laxatives can be used to treat constipation which can cause acute
abdominal pain, however, this man has been opening his bowels
regularly and has signs of peritonism, both of which make constipation
less likely.
PPIs may be useful in the treatment of gastritis which this man is at risk
of due to his history of GORD however again this is not likely to present
with signs of peritonitis and such deranged observations. The pain is
also more likely to be epigastric rather than generalised.
Acute mesenteric ischaemia
Acute mesenteric ischaemia is typically caused by an embolism
resulting in occlusion of an artery which supplies the small bowel, for
example the superior mesenteric artery. Classically patients have a
history of atrial fibrillation.

Question 241 of 267
A 60-year-old woman presents with gradually increasing abdominal
swelling over several years. In recent weeks, she has also noticed a
painful lump in her left groin. She has no significant past medical history
and takes no regular medications.
On abdominal examination, there is abdominal distension with evidence
of shifting dullness and a reducible inguinal hernia.
A CT scan reveals a calcified mass in the appendix and scalloping of the
liver surface.
© Image used on license from Radiopaedia
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
This patient presents with gradual abdominal swelling, ascites, and an
inguinal hernia. The CT findings are consistent with pseudomyxoma
peritonei, an uncommon condition characterised by mucinous ascites,
typically associated with a perforated epithelial neoplasm of the
appendix. The CT scan identified a calcified appendiceal mass, likely the
primary tumour, and scalloping of the liver surface (indentations in the
liver capsule caused by tumour deposits), which is classical.
Management involves surgery and intra-peritoneal chemotherapy.
Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome caused by hormone
release from neuroendocrine tumours. Although the appendix is a
common site for neuroendocrine tumours, the presentation and
radiological findings here are inconsistent with carcinoid syndrome.
Patients with carcinoid syndrome typically present with flushing,
diarrhoea, and wheezing, all of which are absent in this case.
Additionally, ascites and liver scalloping support pseudomyxoma
peritonei rather than carcinoid syndrome.
Colorectal carcinoma usually presents with altered bowel habit, blood in
the stool, weight loss, or features of iron-deficiency anaemia. Some
cases are identified through national screening programmes. While
abdominal distension could be a presenting symptom, it is less typical.
The CT findings are more indicative of pseudomyxoma peritonei than
metastatic colorectal carcinoma, as there is no colonic mass, and the
scalloping of the liver is characteristic of pseudomyxoma peritonei
rather than metastatic deposits.
Ovarian cancer is the primary differential diagnosis to exclude in this
scenario. It often presents with abdominal distension and ascites, along
with symptoms like early satiety and weight loss. While the abdominal
distension could be consistent with either ovarian cancer or
pseudomyxoma peritonei, the development of an inguinal hernia is more
commonly associated with pseudomyxoma peritonei. Furthermore, the
presence of a calcified appendiceal mass and liver scalloping is
consistent with pseudomyxoma peritonei rather than ovarian cancer.
Small bowel lymphoma is rare, typically occurring in the sixth decade
and slightly more common in males. It has a varied presentation,
including abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and gastrointestinal haemorrhage.
Diagnosis is achieved through endoscopic evaluation with pathological
sampling. Although small bowel lymphoma can present with a mass,
there is no evidence of a small bowel mass on the CT scan. In this case,
the CT findings are classical for pseudomyxoma peritonei rather than
small bowel lymphoma.
Pseudomyxoma peritonei
Pseudomyxoma peritonei is a rare mucinous tumour most commonly
arising from the appendix. The disease is characterised by the
accumulation of large amounts of mucinous material in the abdominal
cavity. It is rare, with an incidence of 1-2/1,000,000 per year

Hydatid cysts are endemic in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern
countries. They are caused by the tapeworm parasite Echinococcus
granulosus. An outer fibrous capsule is formed containing multiple small
daughter cysts. These cysts are allergens which precipitate a type 1
hypersensitivity reaction.
Clinical features are as follows:
Up to 90% of cysts occur in the liver and lungs
Can be asymptomatic, or symptomatic if cysts > 5cm in diameter
Morbidity caused by cyst bursting, infection and organ dysfunction
(biliary, bronchial, renal and cerebrospinal fluid outflow obstruction)
In biliary rupture, there may be the classical triad of; biliary colic,
jaundice, and urticaria

explanation:
This patient is suffering from bile acid malabsorption secondary to the
ileal resection he had for Crohn's disease. The ileum is the site where
over 95% of bile acids are reabsorbed, therefore, loss of the ileum or non-
functioning ileum due to disease means bile acids remain in the
gastrointestinal tract, producing watery diarrhoea. The treatment for bile
acid malabsorption is with bile acid sequestrants such as
cholestyramine.
Pancreatic insufficiency such as in pancreatitis can also cause
diarrhoea. The description of diarrhoea in this instance may be of foul-
smelling stool that is difficult to flush (steatorrhoea) due to the fat
content in the stool. This is usually treated with pancreatin (more
commonly known as Creon). In this case, faecal elastase, which is a
measure of pancreatic exocrine function, is normal, making pancreatic
insufficiency unlikely, and so pancreatin is incorrect.
Loperamide is an anti-diarrhoeal that can be used for many causes of
diarrhoea. However, from the presentation, bile acid malabsorption is the
most obvious cause of his symptoms therefore cholestyramine should
be used 1st line rather than loperamide.
Vitamin B12 deficiency is also a consequence of ileal resection as this is
the site where it is absorbed. However, vitamin B12 deficiency would not
give the presenting symptoms and the patient is not anaemic therefore
hydroxocobalamin is not indicated.
Prednisolone can be used for acute flares of Crohn's disease which can
present with diarrhoea. However, the faecal calprotectin, CRP and
platelets (which often rise in inflammation) are normal making an acute
disease flare unlikely; therefore, prednisolone is not indicated.

Bile-acid malabsorption
Bile-acid malabsorption is a cause of chronic diarrhoea. This may be
primary, due to excessive production of bile acid, or secondary to an
underlying gastrointestinal disorder causing reduced bile acid
absorption. It can lead to steatorrhoea and vitamin A, D, E, K
malabsorption.
Secondary causes are often seen in patients with ileal disease, such as
with Crohn's. Other secondary causes include:
cholecystectomy
coeliac disease
small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

the test of choice is SeHCAT
nuclear medicine test using a gamma-emitting selenium molecule in
selenium homocholic acid taurine or tauroselcholic acid (SeHCAT)
scans are done 7 days apart to assess the retention/loss of
radiolabelled
SeHCAT
Management
bile acid sequestrants e.g. cholestyramine

there is no watery exudate which you would expect. Sjogren's syndrome

lack of watery eyes suggests they are dry and this is the likely diagnosis.
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary
cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged
females (female:male ratio of 9:1). The aetiology is not fully understood
although it is thought to be an autoimmune condition. Interlobular bile
ducts become damaged by a chronic inflammatory process causing
progressive cholestasis which may eventually progress to cirrhosis. The
classic presentation is itching in a middle-aged woman
Associations
Sjogren's syndrome (seen in up to 80% of patients)
rheumatoid arthritis
systemic sclerosis
thyroid disease

early: may be asymptomatic (e.g. raised ALP on routine LFTs) or
fatigue, pruritus
Sjogren's syndrome is common in patients with PBC

endoscopic gastric biopsy

What is the most appropriate treatment regimen given the diagnosis?
explanation:
This woman has biopsy-proven gastric MALT lymphoma. The first-line
treatment is eradication of Helicobacter pylori which is associated with
95% of cases. The only option here that consists of a viable Helicobacter
pylori eradication regimen is omeprazole, clarithromycin, and amoxicillin
and therefore this is the correct answer.
Gastric MALT lymphoma - eradicate H. pylori
Endoscopic ablation involves removing tissue as a therapeutic
procedure during endoscopy. This is a common treatment for Barrett's
oesophagus however is not used first-line for gastric MALT lymphomas
and therefore is incorrect.
Endoscopic ligation is a therapeutic procedure for the treatment of
varices. This involves applying bands to veins to reduce the risk of
bleeding. Ligation is not used in the treatment of gastric MALT
lymphomas.
A gastrectomy is a significant surgical procedure and is not usually
required to treat gastric MALT lymphomas. Most show a good response
to Helicobacter pylori eradication and therefore this is a more appropriate
initial management plan.
Omeprazole alone may reduce the symptoms of a gastric MALT
lymphoma but will not result in Helicobacter pylori eradication or the
resolution of the lymphoma. Therefore, the addition of clarithromycin
and amoxicillin is indicated in this instance and omeprazole alone is an
incorrect answer.
Gastric MALT lymphoma
Overview
associated with H. pylori infection in 95% of cases
good prognosis
if low grade then 80% respond to H. pylori eradication
Features
paraproteinaemia may be present

and biopsy results, this lady has likely developed microscopic colitis
which has been known to be linked to selective serotonin reuptake
inhibitors and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory analgesia.
The most important management step would thus be to cease the use
of these medications, as the onset of sertraline has seemed to correlate
to her symptoms.
A gluten-free diet would be appropriate if coeliac disease was suspected
and only once it had been diagnosed. Coeliac disease is a possibility and
additional investigation may be indicated to exclude this. However, in
this case, we are told that the symptoms are correlating with the onset
of sertraline and the histology supports a diagnosis of microscopic
colitis.
Loperamide would only be of symptomatic benefit and not resolve the
underlying cause of the diarrhoea.
Oral prednisolone and IV hydrocortisone are indicated in acute flares of
macroscopic colitis such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's colitis. In this
case, the most important management step would be to stop the
offending agent which could lead to a complete resolution of the
microscopic colitis.
SSRIs are linked to the development of microscopic colitis
Microscopic colitis
Microscopic colitis is a chronic inflammatory condition of the gut. It is
approximately as common as the 'classic' inflammatory bowel diseases
(ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease) and is considered a separate
entity.
It is typically diagnosed around middle age and is more common in
women.
Risk factors
smoking
drugs: NSAIDs, PPIs and SSRIs

watery diarrhoea: usually insidious but more acute presentations
are seen
faecal urgency and incontinence is a frequent feature
abdominal pain
constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, lethargy and

and ANA may also be present

noticed her right arm always shakes as she stretches it out to write on
the blackboard at school. She has also started dropping cups of tea
because of shaking on picking them up. Her balance has become poor
and she now falls over easily when playing hopscotch with the children.
These problems have developed over 14 months slowly. Her
neurological examination reveals a postural tremor of the upper limbs;
right worse than left, as well as a broad-based ataxic gait. She has some
co-existent rigidity of the right upper limb. Slit lamp examination reveals
brown-green deposits in Descemet's membrane of the cornea. The
remainder of the clinical examination is unremarkable. What is the most
appropriate treatment for the underlying condition?
explanation:
The diagnosis is Wilson's disease: an autosomal-recessive condition that
produces neurological, psychiatric, and hepatic dysfunction.
Presentation is usually in children and young adults in the form of a
postural tremor that may look like essential tremor although may also be
much larger in amplitude (wing-beating tremor). Some patients present
with rigidity and bradykinesia or ataxia rather than tremor. Others
present with an acute hepatitis. Clearly in a young adult multiple
Treatment for Wilson's disease is currently penicillamine
sclerosis (MS) is the other differential to exclude neurologically (MS
plaques in the cerebellum are not uncommon), and the give-away here is
the corneal findings described (they could give you a picture of them),
which are typical of Wilson's. The rigidity is also an extrapyramidal
feature that might steer you away from multiple sclerosis (although of
course, basal ganglia plaques would not be impossible).
The pathophysiology is that there is a failure of hepatic excretion of
copper into bile, therefore copper accumulates in the liver and
secondarily suppresses the synthesis of caeruloplasmin (a copper-
carrying blood protein). Eventually, copper spills over into the circulation
and deposits also in the:
basal ganglia - with neurological sequelae
kidneys - causing tubular degeneration and thus a Fanconi
syndrome (aminoaciduria, glycosuria, phosphaturia,
renal tubular acidosis type 2 (proximal), rickets (children) or
osteomalacia (adults))
cornea - with Kayser-Fleischer rings
bones and joints - erosions
parathyroid glands - altered calcium metabolism
Look out for any of these features in a stem.
The first test to pick in an exam stem if you suspect Wilson's disease
should be caeruloplasmin, which will be low (<20 mg/dl), and then an
elevated urine 24-hour copper excretion (>40 micrograms/ml). If the
diagnosis is still not certain, the liver biopsy can be useful: showing
increased hepatic copper levels. However, in reality, these changes can
be non-specific on their own therefore interpretation is made on their
combination alongside the clinical features.
Treatment is with the copper-chelating trientine or penicillamine.
Reference: 1) Neurology: A Clinician's Approach. Cambridge University
Press; 1 edition (18 Nov. 2010). 2) GP Notebook: Wilson's disease.

explanation:
Transient elastography is a non-invasive, rapid, and reliable method for
assessing liver fibrosis by measuring liver stiffness. It provides
quantitative data that correlates well with fibrosis severity, making it an
effective tool for staging liver disease. This patient, who has clinical and
imaging findings suggestive of cirrhosis, is an ideal candidate as he has
no factors that would interfere with measurement accuracy, such as
ascites or severe obesity. The procedure is painless, reproducible, and
avoids the risks of bleeding associated with invasive techniques. It also
allows for ongoing monitoring of fibrosis progression, making it
particularly useful in chronic liver disease management.
CT imaging is primarily used to assess liver morphology, detect
complications such as hepatocellular carcinoma, and evaluate vascular
structures. While it can identify indirect signs of cirrhosis, such as
nodular liver contour and splenomegaly, it does not accurately quantify
fibrosis.
Liver biopsy provides direct histological evaluation of fibrosis and
inflammation but is invasive and associated with risks such as bleeding
and infection. In this patient, thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy
increase the likelihood of complications. Furthermore, biopsy is subject
to sampling error, as fibrosis can be heterogeneously distributed, leading
to potential underestimation or overestimation of disease severity. While
biopsy remains necessary in cases where the underlying liver disease is
uncertain, it is not required for fibrosis staging when non-invasive
alternatives are available.
Serum markers such as APRI and FIB-4 offer a simple and accessible
method for estimating fibrosis but lack the precision needed for detailed
staging. Their values can be influenced by various factors, including
inflammation and hemolysis, leading to variability in results. While they
are useful for initial fibrosis screening or when advanced imaging is
unavailable, they do not provide the detailed structural assessment
required to confidently stage fibrosis in this patient.
Transient elastography may be useful for diagnosing and
monitoring the severity of liver cirrhosis
Endoscopy is essential for detecting esophageal and gastric varices in
patients with cirrhosis and portal hypertension. However, it does not
provide information on liver fibrosis or help confirm the diagnosis. While
this patient has findings suggestive of portal hypertension, variceal
screening is typically performed after cirrhosis is established, rather than
as an initial step in fibrosis assessment.
Liver cirrhosis
Liver cirrhosis remains a significant problem in the developed world,
account for 60,000 deaths in the UK each year.

explanation:
This is a clinical diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome, supported by
relief on defaecation as well as a panel of normal blood tests. The first-
line anti-motility agent for this presentation of diarrhoea would be
loperamide, as recommended by NICE guidelines. Whilst codeine may be
effective in minimising diarrhoea, it has no established roles in the
management of IBS.
Linaclotide is a laxative that is recommended in use of IBS if symptoms
of constipation predominate, if the patient has had constipation for 12
months and if a trial of the more conventional laxatives fail.
Sertraline and amitriptyline are second-line pharmacological treatments
if anti-motility treatment, laxatives and antispasmodics have failed to
improve symptoms.

explanation:
The Truelove and Witts criteria helps to guide physicians in the
management of ulcerative collitis:
Mild: Bowel movements <4/day, temp <37.8 °C, pulse <90/min,
ESR<30mm/hour, No anaemia, no or small amounts of blood in
stool,
Moderate: Bowel movements 4-6, the remainder of the parameters
are the same for mild.
Severe; Bowel movements 6 or more plus one or more of the
systemic features such as: temp >37.8°C, Pulse > 90/min, ESR
>30mm/hour, visible blood in stool and anaemia.
In this scenario, the patient has a severe exacerbation of her disease
despite medical treatment. As a result, early involvement of the
surgeons is paramount as it is likely that she will need surgical
intervention.
Nice state that:
'Assess and document on admission, and then daily, the likelihood
of needing surgery for people admitted to hospital with acute severe
ulcerative colitis.'
'Be aware that there may be an increased likelihood of needing
surgery for people with any of the following:'
stool frequency more than 8 per day
pyrexia
tachycardia
an abdominal X-ray showing colonic dilatation
low albumin, low haemoglobin, high platelet count or C-reactive
protein (CRP) above 45 mg/litre (bear in mind that normal

features of severe disease). This is persisting despite initial treatment
with rectal aminosalicylates. The next step in management is oral

IV steroids are not the correct answer. This is required for severe disease

refractory life-threatening ulcerative colitis in addition to IV steroids and
can also be used to induce remission where steroids are
contraindicated.
Topical steroids are not the right answer. If the patient had a persisting
flare of moderate distal ulcerative colitis despite topical and oral
aminosalicylates, then topical steroids could be added.
If a mild-moderate flare of distal ulcerative colitis doesn't respond to
topical (rectal) aminosalicylates then oral aminosalicylates should
be added

A biopsy is taken and reported as showing subepithelial and lamina

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate first-line

explanation:
The most likely diagnosis here is eosinophilic oesophagitis (EO) as
evidenced by the symptomatology, eosinophilia, gastroscopic and
histological findings.
Topical steroids such as fluticasone and budesonide are the first-line
treatments for EO. EO is poorly understood but thought to be a form of
an allergic reaction occurring within the oesophagus in response to
certain food types.
Ranitidine is incorrect. Acid suppression does form part of the first-line
management of EO, however, omeprazole and lansoprazole would be the
preferred initial options.
Sucralfateis a complex of aluminium and sulphated sucrose, it can be
used in the management of duodenal and gastric ulcers as it forms a
protective layer over the mucosa. It is not commonly used in the
management of EO.
Systemic steroids can be considered in patients with very severe
disease refractory to first-line treatment.
Oesophageal stenting is incorrect. This can be considered if there is no
symptomatic improvement in dysphagia after 12 months of budesonide
induction therapy. Stenting can be used as initial therapy in very high-
grade strictures.
Dietary modification and topical steroids are used in the
management of eosinophilic oesophagitis

screen for this condition in the general population is transferrin
saturation.
Ferritin is incorrect. This may be normal in early disease and is inferior to
the transferrin saturation for screening purposes.
HFE genetic testing is incorrect. Genetic testing is more appropriate if
there is a relevant family history of haemochromatosis, which is not
mentioned here.
Insulin-like growth factor - 1 (IGF-1) is incorrect. This can be used to
screen for acromegaly, which can also cause fatigue and joint pain.
However, the skin and radiographic appearances are more characteristic
of haemochromatosis.
Short synacthen test is incorrect. Addison's can cause skin changes and
fatigue. However, the 9am cortisol and electrolytes are normal, making
this diagnosis unlikely.
Screening for haemochromatosis
general population: transferrin saturation > ferritin
family members: HFE genetic testing

explanation:
Multiple small calcific foci can be seen in the pancreas consistent with a
background of chronic pancreatitis. The history of alcohol excess with
recurrent abdominal pain is also in keeping with this diagnosis.
Chronic pancreatitis
Chronic pancreatitis is an inflammatory condition which can ultimately
affect both the exocrine and endocrine functions of the pancreas.
Around 80% of cases are due to alcohol excess with up to 20% of cases
being unexplained.
Other than alcohol, causes include:
genetic: cystic fibrosis, haemochromatosis
ductal obstruction: tumours, stones, structural abnormalities
including pancreas divisum and annular pancreas
Features
epigastric pain
radiates to the back
typically worse 15 to 30 minutes following a meal
may be relieved by sitting forward
steatorrhoea: symptoms of pancreatic insufficiency usually develop
between 5 and 25 years after the onset of pain
diabetes mellitus develops in the majority of patients. It typically
occurs more than 20 years after symptom begin
Investigation
abdominal x-ray shows pancreatic calcification in 30% of cases
CT is more sensitive at detecting pancreatic calcification. Sensitivity
is 80%, specificity is 85%
functional tests: faecal elastase may be used to assess exocrine
function if imaging inconclusive

have bowel cancer. He does not currently have any clinical features that
would suggest bowel cancer and is taking no medication. His father died
of colon cancer at the age of 49 and his paternal uncle also had bowel
cancer diagnosed at the age of 44. He was previously referred for a
colonoscopy four months ago which was normal.
His abdominal examination is normal. You rearrange for the patient to
have a colonoscopy in 2 years time.
What is the most appropriate next management step?
Check for a mutation in chromosome 5q21
Check for a DNA mismatch repair gene mutation
Perform a computed tomography (CT) with contrast scan of his
abdomen
Check carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level

options: Check for a mutation in chromosome 5q21

Perform a computed tomography (CT) with contrast scan of his abdomen
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis in this instance is hereditary non-polyposis
colorectal cancer, given his strong family history. This accounts for
roughly 2% of all colorectal cancers and is due to a mutation in the DNA
mismatch repair gene. Once a diagnosis has been established, the
preferred treatment is a colonoscopy every 1-3 years.

explanation:
Transient elastography is the correct answer. This patient’s history of
consuming over 50 units of alcohol per week, together with macrocytic
anaemia and an AST: ALT ratio > 2:1, indicates alcohol-related liver
disease. According to NICE guidelines, men drinking more than 50 units
per week should be offered transient elastography (FibroScan) to assess
for fibrosis and cirrhosis. This test is cost-effective in primary care and
can also demonstrate improvements in liver fibrosis after successful
HCV treatment or cessation of alcohol.
AFP measurement would be premature at this stage. The primary
concern is assessing liver fibrosis severity to guide the management of
the newly diagnosed HCV infection, not screening for hepatocellular
carcinoma.
Liver biopsy is inappropriate. While liver biopsy is traditionally
considered the gold standard for evaluating liver fibrosis, it is costly and
invasive. Alternative, non-invasive tests should be performed instead,
such as transient elastography, which could provide an accurate
assessment of the degree of liver fibrosis/cirrhosis.
Pelvi-abdominal US is incorrect. Although ultrasound can identify
steatosis, hepatomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension, it cannot
accurately stage fibrosis, which is crucial for determining disease
severity and treatment approach in HCV infection. It would be more
appropriate as a complementary investigation rather than the primary
tool for disease severity assessment.
Upper endoscopy should be done as a screening for any patient with
compensated liver cirrhosis whose platelets ≤ 150 * 10 /L or liver
stiffness ≥ 20 kPa. In this case, with a normal platelet count, transient
elastography should be done to evaluate for cirrhosis; its liver stiffness
measurement is then used to decide on variceal screening.
Transient elastography may be useful for diagnosing and
monitoring the severity of liver cirrhosis
Liver cirrhosis
Liver cirrhosis remains a significant problem in the developed world,
account for 60,000 deaths in the UK each year.

explanation:
Recent changes in NICE guidelines suggested that when a patient with
IBS has resistant constipation despite using multiple laxatives with
proper doses, linaclotide (which is a guanylate cyclase-C receptor
agonist) should be used as the next step in management. It works by
increasing intestinal fluid secretion and transit and decreases visceral
pain.
Lactulose is not advised by NICE to be given in patients with IBS.
Adding a TCA or SSRI is the next step after linaclotide if it is found
to be of no benefit.

explanation:
SeHCAT is bile acid analogue that can be detected by a nuclear medicine
scan. The SeHCAT test involves a baseline scan, and then a 7-day scan.
A 7-day SeHCAT retention value of less than 15% is generally considered
indicative of bile salt malabsorption.
Treatment of bile salt malabsorption is with cholestyramine, a bile salt
sequestrant.
Bile-acid malabsorption
Bile-acid malabsorption is a cause of chronic diarrhoea. This may be
primary, due to excessive production of bile acid, or secondary to an
underlying gastrointestinal disorder causing reduced bile acid
absorption. It can lead to steatorrhoea and vitamin A, D, E, K
malabsorption.
Secondary causes are often seen in patients with ileal disease, such as
with Crohn's. Other secondary causes include:
cholecystectomy
coeliac disease
small intestinal bacterial overgrowth

explanation:
This clinical picture is strongly suspicious for a variceal upper gastro-
intestinal (GI) bleed, and the principles of management should be initial
resuscitation with intravenous fluids with two large bore cannulas. A
blood transfusion should be arranged, however, although the patient is
supply. An endoscopy should be offered immediately after resuscitation
to all unstable patients for band ligation of the bleed.
NICE guidelines for variceal bleeds recommend both intravenous
terlipressin and antibiotic prophylaxis prior to endoscopy. Of the two,
there is a significant improvement in the rate of patients achieving initial
haemostasis in patients treated with terlipressin due to its vasopressive
effect in decreasing portal hypertension and would be the more
appropriate drug to give first. Terlipressin should be stopped after
definitive haemostasis has been achieved, or after 5 days of therapy. As
this patient has a platelet count of greater than 50 x 109/L a platelet
transfusion is not indicated, however, she is coagulopathic and would
benefit from both vitamin K and fresh frozen plasma.
Intravenous proton pump inhibitors have a limited evidence base in the
pre-endoscopy management of upper GI bleeds in decreasing the
mortality from variceal bleeds, and are not included in the current NICE
guidelines for the management of variceal bleeds.

Acute interstitial nephritis is incorrect. This condition is characterised
by acute inflammation of the renal tubulo-interstitium, commonly
mediated by a hypersensitivity reaction to medications. The classic triad
of clinical features includes rash, joint pain, and eosinophilia. In this
case, the absence of these features makes it a less likely diagnosis.
Acute tubular necrosis is incorrect. Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) is
common in cirrhotic patients, often as a consequence of sepsis,
dehydration or drugs. The patient does not have any of these features to

glomerulonephritis unlikely. This condition would tend to present with
acute renal failure, hypertension, haematuria, and proteinuria.
Type 1 hepatorenal syndrome is incorrect. Type 1 hepatorenal syndrome
is characterised by a rapid decline in renal function making this a less
likely diagnosis in this case.
Hepatorenal syndrome
The management of hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is notoriously difficult.
The ideal treatment is liver transplantation but patients are often too
unwell to have surgery and there is a shortage of donors
The most accepted theory regarding the pathophysiology of HRS is that
vasoactive mediators cause splanchnic vasodilation which in turn
reduces the systemic vascular resistance. This results in 'underfilling' of
the kidneys. This is sensed by the juxtaglomerular apparatus which then
activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, causing renal
vasoconstriction which is not enough to counterbalance the effects of
the splanchnic vasodilation.

explanation:
This patient is suffering a severe acute flare of ulcerative colitis. It would
appear that so far he has been managed appropriately. The British
Society of Gastroenterology recommend the following basic measures
during an acute flare:
1.) Intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement
2.) Blood transfusion if required to maintain a haemoglobin >10g/dL
3.) Intravenous antibiotics ONLY if infection is considered or prior to
surgery
4.) Subcutaneous heparin to reduce the risk of thromboembolism
5.) Intravenous corticosteroids (either hydrocortisone 100mg four
times a day or methylprednisolone 60mg/day)
6.) Flexible sigmoidoscopy and biopsy within 72 hours to confirm
diagnosis and exclude cytomegalovirus infection
7.) Daily monitoring with physical examination, recording of vital
signs, stool chart, bloods (full blood count, c-reactive protein, serum
electrolytes, serum albumin, liver function tests and glucose) and
consider the need for daily abdominal X-ray.
Intravenous steroids are given for five days with no additional benefit
seen beyond seven days.
At day three a c-reactive protein >45 mg/l or a stool frequency of >8/day
predicts the need for surgery in 85% of cases.
The National Institute for Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommends that if
no improvement is seen after 72 hours of intravenous steroid treatment
or if the patient deteriorates at any time despite corticosteroid treatment
then an urgent surgical review is required ciclosporin (2mg/kg/day)
should be added. NICE recommends that in this acute setting infliximab
reserved for patients in whom ciclosporin is contraindicated or clinically
inappropriate.
The NICE guideline is available here:
www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg166/chapter/1-
Recommendations#inducing-remission-in-people-with-ulcerative-colitis

reviewed with the results of his surveillance biopsies. These show high-
grade dysplasia but no evidence of carcinoma. He is asymptomatic
apart from his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease symptoms which are
well controlled on high dose proton pump inhibitor therapy. What
treatment is he most likely to be offered?
Oesophagectomy
Continue high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy
Endoscopic mucosal therapy
Increase frequency of surveillance endoscopies to every 12
months
Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy, regardless of previous
status
Question 265 of 267
A 60-year-old man who is known to have Barrett's oesophagus is
reviewed with the results of his surveillance biopsies. These show high-
grade dysplasia but no evidence of carcinoma. He is asymptomatic
apart from his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease symptoms which are
well controlled on high dose proton pump inhibitor therapy. What
treatment is he most likely to be offered?
options: Continue high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy
Increase frequency of surveillance endoscopies to every 12 months
Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy, regardless of previous status
explanation:
The correct answer is Endoscopic mucosal therapy. In a patient with
Barrett's oesophagus and high-grade dysplasia, endoscopic mucosal
therapy is the recommended treatment option according to UK
guidelines. This is because high-grade dysplasia is considered a
precursor to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, and endoscopic mucosal
therapy can effectively eradicate the dysplastic tissue, reducing the risk
of progression to cancer. There are several types of endoscopic mucosal
therapy, including radiofrequency ablation (RFA) and endoscopic
resection (ER), which can be used alone or in combination depending on
the extent and location of the dysplasia.
Dysplasia on biopsy in Barrett's oesophagus requires an endoscopic
intervention
The option Oesophagectomy is not the first-line treatment for high-grade
dysplasia in Barrett's oesophagus. Although it may be considered in
selected cases where there is a high risk of progression to carcinoma or
when endoscopic therapies have failed or are contraindicated, it carries
significant morbidity and mortality risks compared to less invasive
endoscopic treatments.
Continue high-dose proton pump inhibitor therapy alone would not be
sufficient for managing high-grade dysplasia in Barrett's oesophagus.
While PPIs help control symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease
and may reduce inflammation in the oesophagus, they do not directly
address the presence of high-grade dysplasia or its potential
progression to carcinoma.
Increase frequency of surveillance endoscopies to every 12 months
would also not be an appropriate management strategy for this patient.
While regular surveillance is important for monitoring patients with
Barrett's oesophagus, increasing the frequency of endoscopies without
addressing the underlying high-grade dysplasia does not provide any
therapeutic benefit.
Lastly, Helicobacter pylori eradication therapy, regardless of previous
status, would not be relevant to this patient's management. While H.
pylori infection is a known risk factor for gastric cancer and peptic ulcer
disease, it has not been directly linked to the development or
progression of Barrett's oesophagus or oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
Therefore, eradicating H. pylori would not address the high-grade
dysplasia in this patient's case.
Barrett's oesophagus
Barrett's refers to the metaplasia of the lower oesophageal mucosa, with
the usual squamous epithelium being replaced by columnar epithelium.

This young patient has features of diarrhoea-predominant IBS. Patients

Although there is some evidence patients with IBD may have a genetic
predisposition, it does not follow a mendelian pattern of inheritance.
Despite her family history of IBD, the nature of her symptoms and normal
blood tests make the diagnosis of IBD unlikely and it would not be
appropriate to proceed with a lower GI endoscopy or CT scan at this
stage.
Faecal calprotectin is a test for intestinal inflammation and has been
recommended by NICE as a screening tool for IBD for GPs. It can also be
used to monitor the response to treatment in IBD patients.
(Source: NICE DG11)
Faecal calprotectin
Faecal calprotectin is a test for intestinal inflammation that has been
recommended by NICE as a screening tool for inflammatory bowel
disease (IBD). It can also be used to monitor the response to treatment
in IBD patients.
In adults, it has a sensitivity of 93% and specificity of 96% for IBD. In
children, the specificity falls to around 75%.
In addition to IBD, other causes of a raised faecal calprotectin include:
bowel malignancy
coeliac disease
infectious colitis
Faecal calprotectin is a highly sensitive and specific test for
inflammatory bowel disease

A 78-year-old man comes to the GP with complaints of tiredness and
epigastric pain. The symptoms began 9 months ago and have
progressively worsened. The pain is intermittent, diffuse and rated 4 out
of 10 in intensity. He appears pale and reports passing dark stools.
On examination, his pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 120/70
mmHg. There is epigastric tenderness. Upper GI endoscopy reveals a
mass in the gastric antrum. The biopsy of the mass shows infiltrates of
lymphoid cells. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen reveals normal
lymph nodes.
Which of the following is the best management for this patient?
Amoxicillin, clarithromycin, and omeprazole
Biopsy of regional lymph nodes
Combination chemotherapy
Gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy
Radiation therapy
Question 100 of 267
A 78-year-old man comes to the GP with complaints of tiredness and
epigastric pain. The symptoms began 9 months ago and have
progressively worsened. The pain is intermittent, diffuse and rated 4 out
of 10 in intensity. He appears pale and reports passing dark stools.
On examination, his pulse is 75/min, and blood pressure is 120/70
mmHg. There is epigastric tenderness. Upper GI endoscopy reveals a
mass in the gastric antrum. The biopsy of the mass shows infiltrates of
lymphoid cells. A CT scan of the chest and abdomen reveals normal
lymph nodes.
Which of the following is the best management for this patient?
explanation:
This patient's presentation and biopsy findings are indicative of gastric
MALT lymphoma. Gastric MALT lymphoma is associated with
Helicobacter pylori in most cases. It is treated by eradicating
Helicobacter pylori with a triple-therapy regimen of a proton pump
inhibitor (omeprazole), plus amoxicillin, and either clarithromycin or
metronidazole. The triple therapy is taken orally for seven days.
Gastric MALT lymphoma - eradicate H. pylori
Gastric MALT lymphoma is a slow-growing tumour. Most people have
early-stage (localised) MALT lymphoma when they are diagnosed.
Biopsy of regional lymph nodes does not provide essential information
for the management of this condition.
MALT lymphoma has an excellent prognosis and responds well to
antibiotic treatment. If antibiotic therapy fails, radiotherapy, rituximab
therapy, chemotherapy, or surgery may be considered.
Gastric MALT lymphoma
Overview
associated with H. pylori infection in 95% of cases
good prognosis
if low grade then 80% respond to H. pylori eradication
Features
paraproteinaemia may be present

A 38-year-old ex-intravenous drug user attends the GUM clinic for review.
He describes a history of needle sharing in the past and is no longer
abusing intravenous drugs. He also describes unprotected sexual
intercourse with a number of partners who he no longer is in touch with,
most recently 3 days prior to attending clinic. He has come to clinic after
hearing a recent awareness campaign around the dangers of
undiagnosed hepatitis C. He is currently well and cannot recall ever
being jaundiced.
He has a wide range of investigations as detailed below.
Hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) - positive
Hepatitis C antibodies - positive
HIV antibody negative
p24 antigen negative
Further testing was carried out based on the results above
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HbsAg) negative
Hepatitis B surface antibody (HbsAb) positive
Hepatitis B envelope antigen (HbeAg) negative
Hepatitis C RNA - negative
What is the most accurate profile of the patient detailed above?
HIV negative, Hepatitis B chronic carrier, Hepatitis C chronic
infection
HIV negative, Hepatitis B chronic carrier, Hepatitis C active
infection
HIV negative, Hepatitis B active infection, Hepatitis C
spontaneously cleared
HIV negative, Hepatitis B previous infection, Hepatitis C
spontaneously cleared
HIV negative, Hepatitis B previous infection, Hepatitis C chronic

most recently 3 days prior to attending clinic. He has come to clinic after
hearing a recent awareness campaign around the dangers of
undiagnosed hepatitis C. He is currently well and cannot recall ever
being jaundiced.
He has a wide range of investigations as detailed below.
Hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb) - positive
Hepatitis C antibodies - positive
HIV antibody negative
p24 antigen negative
Further testing was carried out based on the results above
Hepatitis B surface antigen (HbsAg) negative
Hepatitis B surface antibody (HbsAb) positive
Hepatitis B envelope antigen (HbeAg) negative
Hepatitis C RNA - negative
What is the most accurate profile of the patient detailed above?
options: HIV negative, Hepatitis B chronic carrier, Hepatitis C chronic infection
HIV negative, Hepatitis B chronic carrier, Hepatitis C active infection
HIV negative, Hepatitis B active infection, Hepatitis C spontaneously cleared
Hepatitis B serology HIV negative, Hepatitis B previous infection, Hepatitis C spontaneously cleared
HIV negative, Hepatitis B previous infection, Hepatitis C chronic infection
explanation:
In this case, the patient has been exposed and cleared both hepatitis B
and C infections. In this instance, he is not a carrier and therefore not
infectious to others. During this visit to the GUM clinic, he should also be
tested for infections such as syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea.
HIV testing should be done with HIV antibody and p24 antigen testing. It
is not appropriate to use HIV viral loads as a screening test. The
antibody and p24 tests are 4th generation tests that have helped reduce
the time from exposure to being able to prove infection from one month
(with previous 3rd generation tests) to two weeks.
The understanding of both hepatitis B and C serology is important as
both are commonly ordered tests, both in pregnancy screening,
screening for chemotherapy, or for patients with abnormal liver function
tests. The hepatitis C serology is suggestive of exposure to the virus and
subsequent spontaneous clearing. However, it must be noted that Hep C
Antibody testing can throw up false positives (up to 10%). Where Hep C
antibodies are positive and RNA viral load is undetected it may be
appropriate to repeat the antibody test using a different antibody assay.
The false positive rate is thought to be secondary to other similar
antibodies in the circulation. If the patient has Hep C antibodies and is
Hep C RNA positive for more than 2 months they should be considered
for treatment.

explanation:
This patient has a mild-moderate flare of ulcerative colitis and would
benefit from a trial of oral steroids i.e. prednisolone.
If he had features of a moderate-severe flare e.g. tachycardia, fevers,
drop in haemoglobin, bowels opening >6 times per day, ESR > 30 or
changes on abdominal X-ray, then hydrocortisone would be preferable to
prednisolone.
Azathioprine may be useful in the maintenance of remission but is not
indicated in an acute flare.
Surgical intervention is not indicated until steroid therapy has failed or in
severe flares with radiological changes e.g. toxic megacolon.
Infliximab is not indicated unless steroid therapy has failed.

A 54-year-old woman presents to the gastrointestinal clinic with a 4-
month history of abdominal bloating and cramps associated with loose
stools. She denies vomiting but does recall feeling nauseated with a
reduced appetite. Her past medical history includes type 2 diabetes
mellitus for which she takes metformin, gliclazide and long-acting
insulin.
On examination, she is afebrile with a heart rate of 82 beats/min and a
blood pressure of 132/77mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender
with no palpable masses. Her BMI is 25kg/m².
Investigations are requested:
Hydrogen breath test
20 ppm within 1 hour of oral glucose ingestion
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the recommended management for
this patient?
Amoxicillin, metronidazole and omeprazole
Ciprofloxacin
Hydrocortisone
Rifaximin
Vancomycin
Question 141 of 267
A 54-year-old woman presents to the gastrointestinal clinic with a 4-
month history of abdominal bloating and cramps associated with loose
stools. She denies vomiting but does recall feeling nauseated with a
reduced appetite. Her past medical history includes type 2 diabetes
mellitus for which she takes metformin, gliclazide and long-acting
insulin.
On examination, she is afebrile with a heart rate of 82 beats/min and a
blood pressure of 132/77mmHg. Her abdomen is soft and non-tender
with no palpable masses. Her BMI is 25kg/m².
Investigations are requested:
Hydrogen breath test
20 ppm within 1 hour of oral glucose ingestion
Given the likely diagnosis, what is the recommended management for
this patient?
explanation:
Rifaximin is the treatment of choice for small bowel bacterial
overgrowth syndrome
Rifaximin is correct. This patient has symptoms and signs of small
bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome given the history of prolonged
diarrhoea and abdominal pain and bloating. Symptoms can often overlap
with irritable bowel syndrome. However, small bowel bacterial
overgrowth syndrome is caused by excessive bacteria within the small
bowel. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, as seen in this patient's
past medical history. A hydrogen breath test is used in the diagnosis of
small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome with a positive result
indicating the diagnosis. The raised reading seen here further supports
the diagnosis. Rifaximin is used in the management of small bowel
bacterial overgrowth syndrome. It is currently the preferred treatment
recommended by the British Society of Gastroenterology.
Amoxicillin, metronidazole and omeprazole is incorrect. This is used in
the management of infection with Helicobacter pylori. Unlike a positive
hydrogen breath test, Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with a
positive urea breath test. This combination of antibiotics and
omeprazole is not used in the management of small bowel bacterial
overgrowth syndrome.
Ciprofloxacin is incorrect. This is used in the management of urinary
tract infections, diverticulitis and prostatitis. However, it plays no role in
the management of small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome.
Hydrocortisone is incorrect. Corticosteroids are used in the
management of acute flares of inflammatory bowel disease. However,
they are not used in the management of small bowel bacterial
overgrowth syndrome.
Vancomycin is incorrect. This is a second-line option recommended by
the British Society of Gastroenterology. However, it would not be the
initial choice of antibiotic to use.
Small bowel bacterial overgrowth syndrome

This is an important case at recognising the different causes of
abdominal pain. The clearest features are the raised amylase and central
abdominal pain which points towards pancreatitis. Gallstones are the
main cause but this gentleman no obstructing stones and it is a
common physiological finding to find stones in the bladder. The timing
of the pancreatitis coincides with the onset of steroid use. Sepsis is
unlikely since this gentleman was clinically improving but it can be a
cause of acalculous cholecystitis.
Acute pancreatitis: causes
The vast majority of cases in the UK are caused by gallstones and
alcohol.
Popular mnemonic is GET SMASHED

A 55-year-old woman is seen in the gastroenterology clinic with a history
of itching and malaise, having been found to have a persistently elevated
alkaline phosphatase for the last 12 months by her GP. She has a
background in rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies and
smooth muscle antibodies results are as below.
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies
positive
Smooth muscle antibodies
positive
What additional test is required before the diagnosis can be confirmed?
Faecal elastase
Gamma glutamyl-transferase
Liver biopsy
Rheumatoid factor
Ultrasound of abdomen
Question 227 of 267
A 55-year-old woman is seen in the gastroenterology clinic with a history
of itching and malaise, having been found to have a persistently elevated
alkaline phosphatase for the last 12 months by her GP. She has a
background in rheumatoid arthritis. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies and
smooth muscle antibodies results are as below.
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies
positive
Smooth muscle antibodies
positive
What additional test is required before the diagnosis can be confirmed?
explanation:
The diagnosis in this patient is primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) - as
evidenced by her history of autoimmune conditions, her isolated
elevated alkaline phosphatase, and her positive anti-mitochondrial
antibodies. All patients who are suspected to have PBC should have
imaging (either ultrasound or magnetic resonance
cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) to exclude extra-hepatic biliary
obstruction before making the diagnosis.
Imaging is required before making a diagnosis of PBC to exclude
extrahepatic biliary obstruction
Faecal elastase is a test for pancreatic insufficiency and is not indicated
here.
Gamma glutamyl-transferase is likely to be raised in this scenario but it
would not add any diagnostic value to the investigations.
Liver biopsy is not required as the diagnosis can be made based on
positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies combined with the cholestatic
blood picture. A biopsy may occasionally be considered if there is
uncertainty between the diagnoses of PBC and autoimmune hepatitis.
Rheumatoid factor testing would not be needed as the patient is already
known to have established rheumatoid arthritis.
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary biliary cholangitis (previously referred to as primary biliary
cirrhosis) is a chronic liver disorder typically seen in middle-aged
females (female:male ratio of 9:1). The aetiology is not fully understood
although it is thought to be an autoimmune condition. Interlobular bile
ducts become damaged by a chronic inflammatory process causing
progressive cholestasis which may eventually progress to cirrhosis. The
classic presentation is itching in a middle-aged woman
Associations
Sjogren's syndrome (seen in up to 80% of patients)
rheumatoid arthritis
systemic sclerosis
thyroid disease
Clinical features
